questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.10 Counting principles, permutations and combinations
questions.question:
$n$ points are placed on a circle and every pair of points is joined by a straight chord. Throughout, assume first that the points are in general position, meaning that no three of the chords are concurrent at a point strictly inside the circle.

(a)

Show that, for $n\geq4$ points in general position, the number of intersection points of the chords that lie strictly inside the circle is $\dbinom{n}{4}$.

[4]

(b)

Hence determine the least value of $n$ for which the number of interior intersection points exceeds $1000$.

[3]

(c)

Now suppose the six points are the vertices of a regular hexagon. Explain why $\dbinom{6}{4}=15$ is not the number of distinct interior intersection points, identifying precisely which intersections coincide.

[4]

(d)

Hence determine the number of distinct interior intersection points for the regular hexagon, justifying why no further coincidences occur.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Take any set of four of the points. The four points form a cyclic quadrilateral, and the two diagonals of that quadrilateral are chords which cross at a point strictly inside the circle. (M1) So each $4$-element subset of the points produces at least one interior intersection point.

Conversely, take any interior intersection point. It is the meeting of two chords, and those two chords have four distinct endpoints among the given points, so they determine a unique $4$-element subset. (M1) Within that subset the two crossing chords must be the diagonals rather than the sides, so the intersection produced by the subset is exactly the one we started with.

The correspondence between $4$-element subsets and interior intersection points is therefore a bijection. (A1) Hence the number of interior intersection points equals the number of ways of choosing four points from $n$, namely $\dbinom{n}{4}$. (A1) *(AG)*

(b) We need the least integer $n$ with $\dbinom{n}{4}>1000$. (M1) Now $\dbinom{13}{4}=715$ and $\dbinom{14}{4}=1001$. (A1) Since $\dbinom{n}{4}$ increases with $n$ for $n\geq4$, the least such value is $n=14$. (A1)

(c) Label the vertices $V_0,V_1,\dots,V_5$ in order. The three chords $V_0V_3$, $V_1V_4$ and $V_2V_5$ join opposite vertices, so each is a diameter of the circumcircle and all three pass through the centre $O$. (M1) The general-position formula counts each *pair* of crossing chords separately: these three chords contribute the three crossing pairs $(V_0V_3,V_1V_4)$, $(V_0V_3,V_2V_5)$ and $(V_1V_4,V_2V_5)$ to $\dbinom{6}{4}$. (A1) But all three pairs meet at the single point $O$, so the formula counts $O$ three times when it should count it once, an overcount of $2$. (A1) Checking the remaining crossing pairs shows that no two of them meet at the same interior point, so this is the only coincidence. (A1)

(d) Start from the $\dbinom{6}{4}=15$ crossing pairs. The three crossing pairs of diameters do not give three points but one, so replacing those three points by the single point $O$ reduces the total by $3-1=2$. (M1)(A1) Therefore the number of distinct interior intersection points is $15-2=13$, that is $15-3+1=13$. (M1)(A1)(A1) The twelve remaining crossing pairs each give a distinct point, and none of them lies at $O$, so the correction is complete.
questions.explanation:
Two ideas are tested here, and they pull in opposite directions. The first is that counting can be done by finding the right bijection rather than by counting objects directly: instead of counting intersections, count the $4$-element subsets that produce them. The second is that a formula proved under a general-position hypothesis can fail the moment the hypothesis is dropped, and the failure has to be quantified rather than guessed.

The general-position hypothesis, that no three chords are concurrent, is exactly what makes the bijection exact. It is easy to forget that the hypothesis is doing work. Most candidates use it in part (a) without noticing, then apply $\dbinom{6}{4}$ to the regular hexagon in part (c) as though nothing had changed. That is the trap.

Why the regular hexagon rather than, say, a pentagon? Because the hexagon is the smallest regular polygon in which three diagonals are concurrent at an interior point. For $n=4$ and $n=5$ there is no such concurrence and the formula is exact, and the heptagon and nonagon also happen to have no interior triple points. The hexagon is therefore the first genuine counterexample, and it is small enough to draw and check by hand.

The correction is a small inclusion-exclusion. Three crossing pairs collapse onto one point, so three points become one and the count drops by two. The answer is $15-3+1=13$, not $15-3=12$: the difference is whether the surviving centre point is counted at all. Candidates who write $12$ have removed the centre entirely.

The classic wrong turns are: counting all $\dbinom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}$ pairs of chords, which includes chords sharing an endpoint and chords meeting outside the circle; assuming the hexagon has the same count as the general-position case; and subtracting three rather than two. A useful check is that the hexagon must have fewer than $15$ distinct interior points but more than $10$, since the only collapse is at the centre.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.12 Complex numbers; 1.13 Modulus-argument form
questions.question:
Let $z$ be a complex number and let $\bar z$ denote its complex conjugate.

(a)

By writing $z=a+bi$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, solve the equation $z^{2}=\bar z$, giving every solution in the form $a+bi$.

[4]

(b)

Show that every non-zero solution of $z^{2}=\bar z$ satisfies $|z|=1$, and deduce that every non-zero solution is a cube root of unity.

[3]

(c)

Hence, using modulus-argument form, solve the equation $z^{n}=\bar z$ for a general integer $n\geq1$, and state how many solutions it has.

[4]

(d)

Determine the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $z^{n}=\bar z$ has a solution whose real part is exactly $\dfrac12$, and describe all such integers $n$.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Put $z=a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $z^{2}=(a^{2}-b^{2})+2abi$ and $\bar z=a-bi$. (M1) Equating real and imaginary parts,

$$a^{2}-b^{2}=a,\qquad 2ab=-b.$$ (A1)

The second equation gives $b(2a+1)=0$, so either $b=0$ or $a=-\tfrac12$.

If $b=0$, then $a^{2}=a$, so $a=0$ or $a=1$, giving $z=0$ and $z=1$. (A1)

If $a=-\tfrac12$, then $a^{2}-b^{2}=a$ gives $\tfrac14-b^{2}=-\tfrac12$, so $b^{2}=\tfrac34$ and $b=\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, giving $z=-\tfrac12\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$. (A1)

The solutions are $z=0$, $z=1$, $z=-\tfrac12+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$ and $z=-\tfrac12-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$.

(b) Let $z\neq0$ satisfy $z^{2}=\bar z$. Taking moduli, $|z^{2}|=|\bar z|$, so $|z|^{2}=|z|$. Since $|z|\neq0$ we may divide, giving $|z|=1$. (M1)(A1) Then

$$z^{3}=z\cdot z^{2}=z\bar z=|z|^{2}=1.$$ (A1)

So every non-zero solution satisfies $z^{3}=1$, that is, is a cube root of unity. Indeed the three non-zero solutions found in (a) are $1$, $e^{2\pi i/3}$ and $e^{4\pi i/3}$.

(c) Write $z=re^{i\theta}$ with $r\geq0$. Then $z^{n}=r^{n}e^{in\theta}$ and $\bar z=re^{-i\theta}$. (M1) Equating moduli gives $r^{n}=r$, so $r=0$ or $r=1$. (A1)

If $r=0$ then $z=0$, which satisfies the equation. If $r=1$ then $e^{in\theta}=e^{-i\theta}$, so $e^{i(n+1)\theta}=1$, giving $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi k}{n+1}$ for $k=0,1,\dots,n$. (A1) Hence the non-zero solutions are the $n+1$ roots of $z^{n+1}=1$, and together with $z=0$ the equation has $n+2$ solutions. (A1)

(d) A solution with real part $\tfrac12$ cannot be $z=0$, so by the argument in (b) it has $|z|=1$. (M1) Writing $z=e^{i\theta}$ with $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$ gives $\theta=\pm\tfrac{\pi}{3}+2\pi m$, so $z=e^{\pm i\pi/3}$, a primitive sixth root of unity. (A1)

From (c), the solutions of $z^{n}=\bar z$ are $0$ together with the $(n+1)$th roots of unity. So $e^{i\pi/3}$ is a solution exactly when it is an $(n+1)$th root of unity, that is when $\left(e^{i\pi/3}\right)^{n+1}=1$, which is $e^{i\pi(n+1)/3}=1$, so $\dfrac{n+1}{3}$ must be an even integer. (M1)

Hence $n+1$ is a multiple of $6$, that is $n\equiv5\pmod6$. (A1) The smallest such integer is $n=5$; indeed $z=e^{i\pi/3}$ satisfies $z^{5}=e^{i5\pi/3}=e^{-i\pi/3}=\bar z$. All integers $n=5,11,17,23,\dots$ work. (A1)
questions.explanation:
Parts (a) and (b) are algebraic and accessible; the question becomes hard at (c) and (d), where the same equation has to be understood structurally rather than solved case by case.

The unifying observation is that $\bar z=\dfrac{|z|^{2}}{z}$ for $z\neq0$. Substituting into $z^{n}=\bar z$ gives $z^{n+1}=|z|^{2}$, so on taking moduli $|z|^{n+1}=|z|^{2}$, which forces $|z|=1$ (or $z=0$). Once $|z|=1$ we have $\bar z=\dfrac1z$, and the equation becomes $z^{n+1}=1$. The whole problem collapses to a statement about roots of unity: the solutions are $0$ together with the $(n+1)$th roots of unity. This is the insight that part (c) is designed to make unavoidable, and it explains why part (b) asks about $|z|=1$: that is the hinge.

Part (d) inverts the question. Instead of solving for $z$ given $n$, it fixes a property of $z$, namely real part $\tfrac12$, and asks which $n$ allow it. The set of solutions is a cyclic group of order $n+1$; a real part of $\tfrac12$ means the solution is $e^{\pm i\pi/3}$, a primitive sixth root of unity. For this element to lie in the group of order $n+1$, the order must be divisible by $6$, giving $n\equiv5\pmod6$. The answer is an arithmetic progression, which is the kind of result that appears only once the group structure is visible.

Classic wrong turns: dividing the imaginary equation by $b$ in (a) and losing two solutions; using polar form in (c) but forgetting $z=0$; assuming in (d) that a solution with real part $\tfrac12$ must be found by solving one fixed equation rather than searching over $n$; and concluding that only $n=5$ works, missing the infinite family. A useful check is that $n=1$ gives $z=\bar z$, whose solutions are all real, so none has real part $\tfrac12$, consistent with $1\not\equiv5\pmod6$.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 3.12 Vectors, position vectors and displacement; 3.15 Configurations of lines in space
questions.question:
Relative to an origin $O$, the point $A$ has position vector $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and the point $B$ has position vector $\mathbf{b}(k)=\begin{pmatrix}k\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$, where $k$ is a real parameter. The line $L_{1}$ passes through $A$ and has direction vector $\mathbf{u}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$; the line $L_{2}$ passes through $B(k)$ and has direction vector $\mathbf{v}(k)=\begin{pmatrix}2k\\k\\k-1\end{pmatrix}$.

(a)

Show that the displacement vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is $\begin{pmatrix}k\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$, and show that the scalar triple product $(\mathbf{b}(k)-\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}(k))$ equals $k(k-1)$.

[3]

(b)

Hence determine the two values of $k$ for which $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are coplanar, and explain why a vanishing scalar triple product cannot by itself distinguish parallel lines from intersecting lines.

[3]

(c)

For $k=1$, determine the relationship between $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$, deciding in particular whether the two lines coincide, and justify your conclusion fully.

[4]

(d)

For $k=0$, show that $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ intersect, and determine the position vector of their point of intersection.

[3]

(e)

Hence classify the relationship between $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ for every real value of $k$, stating clearly the values of $k$ for which the lines are skew.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The displacement from $A$ to $B(k)$ is

$$\overrightarrow{AB(k)}=\mathbf{b}(k)-\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}k\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}k\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}.$$ (M1)

The vector product of the two direction vectors is

$$\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}(k)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}2k\\k\\k-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1(k-1)-0(k)\\0(2k)-2(k-1)\\2(k)-1(2k)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}k-1\\-2(k-1)\\0\end{pmatrix}=(k-1)\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}.$$ (M1)

Hence

$$(\mathbf{b}(k)-\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}(k))=\begin{pmatrix}k\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}\cdot(k-1)\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}=(k-1)(k)=k(k-1).$$ (A1) *(AG)*

(b) The two lines are coplanar exactly when this scalar triple product vanishes, so $k(k-1)=0$, giving $k=0$ or $k=1$. (A1) The triple product measures whether the displacement $\overrightarrow{AB(k)}$ lies in the plane spanned by the two direction vectors. (R1) When it is zero the three vectors are linearly dependent and the lines lie in one common plane, but inside a common plane two lines either meet at a single point or are parallel (possibly coincident). Both alternatives make the triple product zero, so its value cannot separate them, and an independent test on the direction vectors is required. (A1)

(c) Setting $k=1$ gives $\mathbf{v}(1)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{u}$, so the direction vectors are parallel and therefore the lines are parallel. (A1) This is consistent with the triple product vanishing at $k=1$, and it shows that the zero located in part (b) does not mean that the lines meet. (R1) To decide between distinct and coincident lines, test whether $B(1)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$ lies on $L_{1}$. (M1) Every point of $L_{1}$ has the form $\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, so its $z$-coordinate is always $1$, whereas $B(1)$ has $z$-coordinate $0$; equivalently, $\overrightarrow{AB(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ is not a multiple of $\mathbf{u}$, since $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\neq\mathbf{0}$. (A1) Hence for $k=1$ the lines are parallel and distinct; they do not coincide.

(d) When $k=0$ we have $B(0)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v}(0)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$, which is not a multiple of $\mathbf{u}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, so the lines are not parallel. (M1) Since part (b) shows that they are coplanar at $k=0$, they must meet at a single point. Writing

$$\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix},$$

the $x$-component gives $2s=0$, so $s=0$; the $y$-component $s=0$ is then satisfied automatically; and the $z$-component gives $1=-t$, so $t=-1$. (M1) The unique intersection point is $\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$, which is the point $A$ itself. (A1)

(e) For every $k\notin\{0,1\}$ the triple product equals $k(k-1)\neq0$, so the lines are not coplanar and are therefore skew. (A1) At $k=1$ the lines are parallel and distinct, and at $k=0$ they intersect at $A$. (A1) Parallelism occurs only at $k=1$, and there the lines do not share a point, so no value of $k$ makes the lines coincide. (A1)

Summary: $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are skew for all $k\neq0,1$; parallel and distinct for $k=1$; intersecting at $\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ for $k=0$; and never coincident.
questions.explanation:
Two syllabus ideas meet here. From 3.12 the student must form a displacement vector from two position vectors and use it, together with the two direction vectors, to test the relative position of two lines. From 3.15 the student must then interpret the result: coincident, parallel, intersecting or skew.

The scalar triple product is the standard test, and its most common use is the opposite of this question. If it is non-zero the lines are skew, and if it is zero they are coplanar. The trap lies in the second case. A vanishing triple product says only that the three vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are linearly dependent, that is, that the two lines lie in one plane. Inside a plane two lines either cross or are parallel; both make the triple product zero. So the test is genuinely inconclusive whenever it returns zero, and a second, independent check is needed.

Here the inconclusiveness is doubled, because $T(k)=k(k-1)$ vanishes at two different values of $k$ for two different reasons. At $k=1$ the direction vector $\mathbf{v}(1)$ equals $\mathbf{u}$, so the lines are parallel: the triple product is zero because the cross product itself is zero, not because the lines meet. The student must then test coincidence, and the point $B(1)$ has $z$-coordinate $0$ while every point of $L_{1}$ has $z$-coordinate $1$, so the lines are parallel and distinct. At $k=0$ the direction vectors are not parallel, so coplanarity now does force an intersection, which turns out to be the point $A$ itself. For all other values of $k$ the triple product is non-zero and the lines are skew.

The classic wrong turns are: concluding from $T=0$ that the lines intersect, without checking the directions; concluding 'coincident' at $k=1$ merely because the direction vectors are equal; and forgetting that the displacement used in the test must join a point of one line to a point of the other, not two arbitrary points. A useful check is the count of cases: with two lines in space there are four possibilities, and the answer should exhibit three of them here, with coincidence correctly ruled out.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.4 Financial applications of geometric sequences and series
questions.question:
A loan of €45 000 is taken at a nominal annual rate of 6.0%, compounded monthly, so the monthly rate is 0.5%. It is repaid by equal monthly payments of €900, the first payment being made one month after the loan is taken.

(a)

Show that the outstanding balance immediately after the $n$th payment is $B_n = 45000(1.005)^n - 180000\left((1.005)^n - 1\right)$.

[4]

(b)

Determine the number of full payments of €900 that are required to repay the loan.

[4]

(c)

Determine the amount of the final, smaller payment and the total interest paid over the life of the loan.

[5]

(d)

A second borrower makes $58$ payments of €900 and then receives a refund of the overpayment. Calculate the size of that refund.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) After one month the balance is $45000(1.005) - 900$. (M1) Each subsequent month multiplies the previous balance by $1.005$ and subtracts $900$, so after $n$ payments $B_n = 45000(1.005)^n - 900(1 + 1.005 + \cdots + 1.005^{n-1})$. (M1) The bracket is a geometric series with common ratio $1.005$, so it equals $\frac{(1.005)^n - 1}{0.005}$. (M1) Since $900 / 0.005 = 180000$, this gives $B_n = 45000(1.005)^n - 180000\left((1.005)^n - 1\right)$. (AG) The derivation shows that the balance equals the accumulated value of the loan less the accumulated value of the payments.

(b) Substituting $n = 57$ gives $B_{57} = 45000(1.005)^{57} - 180000\left((1.005)^{57} - 1\right) = 609.5627\ldots$, which is positive. (M1)(A1) Substituting $n = 58$ gives $B_{58} = -287.3895\ldots$, which is negative. (M1) Hence $57$ full payments are made and the loan is cleared by the next payment. (A1) The small positive balance signals that the end of the loan is close.

(c) The final payment is one further month of interest on the balance after the $57$th payment, so it equals $B_{57} \times 1.005 = 612.610485\ldots$, that is €612.61 to the nearest cent. (M1)(A1) This is smaller than €900, as required. (R1) The final payment is not €900; it is the balance remaining after the fifty-seventh payment together with one further month of interest. The total repaid is $57 \times 900 + 612.61 = 51912.61$ euro. (M1) The total interest is therefore $51912.61 - 45000 = 6912.61$ euro. (A1)

(d) If $58$ payments of €900 are made, the total paid is $58 \times 900 = 52200$ euro. (M1) The overpayment is $52200 - 51912.61 = 287.39$ euro. (A1) This agrees with $-B_{58} = 287.3895\ldots$, which confirms the refund. (R1)
questions.explanation:
The question is an amortisation problem, but its twist is the final instalment. The standard treatment assumes every payment is €900; here the loan is not cleared exactly, so after some number of full payments a residue remains and the last payment is smaller. The candidate has to find where that residue sits rather than force the payments to fit.

Part (a) builds the balance from first principles. Each month the debt grows by the factor $1.005$ and then loses €900, and unrolling the recursion leaves a geometric series of payments. Summing that series and using $900 / 0.005 = 180000$ produces the closed form $B_n = 45000(1.005)^n - 180000((1.005)^n - 1)$. Everything after this is arithmetic on that expression.

Part (b) is the locating step. At $n = 57$ the balance is still positive at €609.56, but at $n = 58$ it has overshot to €-287.39. So $57$ full payments are possible and the $58$th cannot be made in full, which is exactly the situation the question is built around.

Part (c) computes the final payment correctly by allowing the outstanding balance one more month of interest: $B_{57} \times 1.005 = 612.61$, which is smaller than €900. The total interest is then the sum of all payments minus the principal, €6912.61. A larger instalment would clear the debt sooner, while a smaller one would never clear it. Part (d) contrasts this with a borrower who simply makes $58$ full payments and is refunded the excess; the refund is the same €287.39 that appears as $-B_{58}$. The classic errors are assuming the $58$th payment is €900, rounding the balance to cents before multiplying by $1.005$, and computing interest as a percentage of the principal rather than as total payments minus the loan.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.8 Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences and 1.3 Geometric sequences and series
questions.question:
A geometric series has second term $-6$ and sum to infinity $8$. Its first term is $a$ and its common ratio is $r$.

(a)

Given that the second term is $-6$ and the sum to infinity is $8$, show that $4r^2 - 4r - 3 = 0$.

[4]

(b)

Hence find the two possible values of the common ratio $r$.

[3]

(c)

Determine which of these two values of $r$ is admissible for a convergent series, and find the corresponding first term $a$ and third term $ar^2$.

[5]

(d)

Find the sum of the first ten terms of the convergent series, giving your answer as an exact fraction.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The second term is $ar = -6$, so $a = -6/r$. (M1) The two relations $ar = -6$ and $a/(1-r) = 8$ are the only information available, so eliminating $a$ is the natural first move. Substituting this into the sum to infinity $a/(1-r) = 8$ gives $-6/r = 8(1-r)$, so $-6 = 8r(1-r)$. (M1) Expanding the right-hand side, $-6 = 8r - 8r^2$, and bringing every term to one side gives $8r^2 - 8r - 6 = 0$. (A1) Dividing through by $2$ yields $4r^2 - 4r - 3 = 0$, as required. (AG)

(b) Factorising, $4r^2 - 4r - 3 = (2r - 3)(2r + 1)$. (M1) Setting each factor to zero gives $2r - 3 = 0$ or $2r + 1 = 0$, so $r = 3/2$ or $r = -1/2$. (A1) Both values satisfy the quadratic, which substitution confirms. (A1)

(c) A geometric series converges to a finite sum only when $|r| < 1$. (R1) For $r = 3/2$ we have $|r| = 1.5 > 1$, so this series diverges and cannot have sum to infinity $8$; that root must be rejected. (R1) For $r = -1/2$ we have $|r| = 0.5 < 1$, so this is the admissible value. (A1) Then $a = -6/(-1/2) = 12$, and the third term is $ar^2 = 12(1/4) = 3$. (A1) Checking the sum, $12/(1 - (-1/2)) = 12/(3/2) = 8$, as required. (A1)

(d) The sum of the first $n$ terms is $S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)$. (M1) With $a = 12$, $r = -1/2$ and $n = 10$, this is $S_{10} = 12(1 - (-1/2)^{10})/(1 + 1/2)$. (M1) Now $(-1/2)^{10} = 1/1024$ and $1 + 1/2 = 3/2$, so $S_{10} = 12(1023/1024)/(3/2) = 8(1023/1024)$. (A1) Hence $S_{10} = 8184/1024 = 1023/128$. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the algebra of part (a) and the convergence condition of part (c) pull in opposite directions. The substitution $ar = -6$ into $a/(1-r) = 8$ is standard, and it produces a quadratic whose two roots are both genuine roots of that quadratic; nothing in the algebra of parts (a) and (b) can tell the candidate which one is wanted. The decisive fact is that a geometric series has a finite sum to infinity only when $|r| < 1$, so the root $r = 3/2$ is a valid solution of the equation but not a valid common ratio for a convergent series. This is the trap: a candidate who stops at part (b) and reports both roots has answered a different question from the one asked.

The negative ratio $r = -1/2$ then has to be carried forward correctly. The first term follows from $a = -6/r = 12$, the third term from $ar^2 = 3$, and the check $12/(1 + 1/2) = 8$ confirms that the reconstructed series really does have the stated sum. Part (d) rewards exactness: the alternating ratio makes $(-1/2)^{10}$ positive, so the finite sum is slightly below $8$, and the exact value is $1023/128$. A candidate who works with decimals will see $7.9921875$ and may not recognise the fraction, which is why the command term insists on an exact fraction. The rejection of the positive root is the whole point of the exercise: an examiner expects the candidate to say explicitly that $|r| > 1$ prevents convergence, not merely to discard the root because it looks large. Both roots solve the quadratic, so the arithmetic alone cannot separate them, and a final check that the surviving series really does sum to $8$ closes the argument.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.9 The binomial theorem
questions.question:
In the expansion of $(1 + x/2)^n$, where $n$ is a positive integer, the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^5$ are equal.

(a)

Given that the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^5$ are equal, show that $n = 14$.

[4]

(b)

Find the greatest coefficient in the expansion, stating the term or terms at which it occurs.

[6]

(c)

Hence find the coefficient of $x^6$ in the expansion of $(1 + x/2)^{14}(1 - x)^3$.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) The general term of the expansion is $\binom{n}{r}(x/2)^r$, so the coefficient of $x^r$ is $\binom{n}{r}/2^r$. (M1) Equating the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^5$ gives $\binom{n}{4}/2^4 = \binom{n}{5}/2^5$. (M1) Multiplying by $2^5$ and dividing by $\binom{n}{5}$ gives $\binom{n}{4}/\binom{n}{5} = 1/2$. (M1) Now $\binom{n}{4}/\binom{n}{5} = 5/(n-4)$, so $5/(n-4) = 1/2$. (A1) Hence $n - 4 = 10$ and $n = 14$, as required. (AG)

(b) Write $t_r = \binom{14}{r}/2^r$ for the coefficient of $x^r$. (M1) The ratio of consecutive coefficients is $t_{r+1}/t_r = (1/2)\binom{14}{r+1}/\binom{14}{r} = (1/2)(14-r)/(r+1)$. (M1) This ratio is at least $1$ exactly when $14 - r \ge 2(r+1)$, that is $14 - r \ge 2r + 2$, so $r \le 4$. (A1) The coefficients therefore increase up to $r = 4$, and at $r = 4$ the ratio equals $1$, so $t_4 = t_5$; for $r > 4$ the ratio is below $1$ and the coefficients decrease. (R1) The greatest coefficient is thus $t_4 = \binom{14}{4}/2^4 = 1001/16 = 62.5625$. (A1) It is attained twice, by the terms in $x^4$ and $x^5$, since $t_5 = \binom{14}{5}/2^5 = 2002/32 = 1001/16$. (A1) Because the ratio equals exactly $1$ at $r = 4$, the two largest coefficients are equal and every other coefficient is strictly smaller. For comparison, $t_3 = 364/8 = 45.5$ and $t_6 = 3003/64 = 46.921875$, both smaller. (R1)

(c) Expanding, $(1 - x)^3 = 1 - 3x + 3x^2 - x^3$. (M1) If $a_r$ denotes the coefficient of $x^r$ in $(1 + x/2)^{14}$, then the coefficient of $x^6$ in the product is $a_6 - 3a_5 + 3a_4 - a_3$. (M1) Substituting, this is $3003/64 - 3(1001/16) + 3(1001/16) - 364/8$. (A1) The two middle terms cancel exactly, leaving $3003/64 - 364/8$. (A1) Writing over the common denominator $64$, this is $3003/64 - 2912/64 = 91/64$. (A1) Hence the coefficient is $91/64 = 1.421875$. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The stem is a coefficient-matching problem, but the equality of two coefficients is only the entry point; the real work is deciding where the coefficients stop growing. In part (a) the factors $2^r$ from $(x/2)^r$ must be carried into the comparison, and it is the ratio $\binom{n}{4}/\binom{n}{5} = 5/(n-4)$ that reduces the condition to a one-line equation. The common error is to compare binomial coefficients alone, which shifts the answer from $n = 14$ to $n = 9$ and destroys the later parts.

Part (b) turns on the ratio of consecutive coefficients, $t_{r+1}/t_r = (1/2)(14-r)/(r+1)$. The coefficients increase while this ratio exceeds $1$ and decrease once it falls below $1$, and the critical case is when the ratio equals $1$ exactly: that happens at $r = 4$, so the maximum is shared by the terms in $x^4$ and $x^5$. This tie is the twist, because a candidate who assumes a single greatest term will report only one of the two.

Part (c) hides a designed cancellation. Multiplying by $(1-x)^3$ mixes four consecutive coefficients with alternating signs, and because $a_4 = a_5$ the two middle contributions cancel exactly, leaving only $a_6 - a_3$. The result $91/64$ is far smaller than the individual coefficients, which is a strong signal that the cancellation was intended. Truncating the product or mis-signed terms give answers of a completely different size. The candidate is also expected to recognise that the tie at $r = 4$ is exact rather than approximate, because the ratio equals $1$ precisely there; this is why the maximum is shared by two terms and not attained at a single index. Reporting only $t_4$ or only $t_5$ therefore answers only half of the question, and the markscheme requires both to be named explicitly.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.4 Key features of graphs and 2.8 The reciprocal function
questions.question:
The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = \frac{2x + 3}{x - 1}$.

(a)

Determine the equations of the asymptotes and the coordinates of the intercepts of the graph of $y = f(x)$.

[4]

(b)

Find an expression for $\frac{1}{f(x)}$ in the form $\frac{x+a}{bx+c}$, and state the equations of its asymptotes and the coordinates of its intercepts.

[4]

(c)

Explain how the asymptotes and intercepts of $y = \frac{1}{f(x)}$ relate to those of $y = f(x)$.

[3]

(d)

Solve the inequality $f(x) \ge \frac{1}{f(x)}$, giving your answer in interval notation.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) A vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator vanishes, so $x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = 1$. (A1) The function is undefined there, so $x = 1$ is excluded from the domain. Dividing, $\frac{2x+3}{x-1} = 2 + \frac{5}{x-1}$, so as $x \to \pm\infty$ the graph approaches $y = 2$; this is the horizontal asymptote. (A1) The $y$-intercept is $f(0) = 3/(-1) = -3$, giving $(0, -3)$. (A1) The $x$-intercept solves $2x + 3 = 0$, so $x = -3/2$, giving $(-3/2, 0)$. (A1)

(b) Taking the reciprocal, $\frac{1}{f(x)} = \frac{x-1}{2x+3}$. (M1) This has the form $\frac{x+a}{bx+c}$ with $a = -1$, $b = 2$, $c = 3$. (A1) Its vertical asymptote is $x = -3/2$, where the denominator vanishes, and its horizontal asymptote is $y = 1/2$, the ratio of the leading coefficients. (A1) The $y$-intercept is $(0, -1/3)$ and the $x$-intercept is $(1, 0)$. (A1)

(c) The $x$-intercept of $f$ at $x = -3/2$ becomes the vertical asymptote of $1/f$, and the vertical asymptote of $f$ at $x = 1$ becomes the $x$-intercept of $1/f$; in other words, the zeros and the poles swap roles. (R1) The horizontal asymptote changes from $y = 2$ to its reciprocal $y = 1/2$. (R1) The $y$-intercept changes from $-3$ to its reciprocal $-1/3$, since $1/f(0) = 1/(-3)$. (R1)

(d) The inequality is $\frac{2x+3}{x-1} \ge \frac{x-1}{2x+3}$. (M1) Subtracting the right-hand side and combining over the common denominator $(x-1)(2x+3)$ gives $\frac{(2x+3)^2 - (x-1)^2}{(x-1)(2x+3)} \ge 0$. (M1) The numerator factorises as $\left[(2x+3) - (x-1)\right]\left[(2x+3) + (x-1)\right] = (x+4)(3x+2)$. (A1) So the inequality is $\frac{(x+4)(3x+2)}{(x-1)(2x+3)} \ge 0$. (A1) The critical values are $-4$, $-3/2$, $-2/3$ and $1$, and a sign table gives the solution $(-\infty, -4] \cup (-3/2, -2/3] \cup (1, \infty)$; the endpoints $-4$ and $-2/3$ are included because the numerator vanishes there, while $-3/2$ and $1$ are excluded because the expression is undefined there. (A1)
questions.explanation:
Reciprocating a function rearranges its graph in a very specific way, and the item is designed so that this rearrangement is the object of study rather than a by-product. In part (a) the rational function is read for its asymptotes and intercepts; rewriting it as $2 + 5/(x-1)$ makes the horizontal asymptote immediate and shows that the graph is a shifted hyperbola.

Part (b) asks for $1/f$ explicitly, and the key observation is that the reciprocal of a rational function is obtained by swapping numerator and denominator. The consequence is a complete exchange of roles: the zero of $f$ at $x = -3/2$ becomes the pole of $1/f$, and the pole of $f$ at $x = 1$ becomes the zero of $1/f$. The horizontal asymptote changes to the reciprocal of the original one, and the $y$-intercept changes to the reciprocal of the original intercept. Part (c) asks the candidate to state this pattern, which is where the structural understanding is assessed.

Part (d) turns the comparison $f(x) \ge 1/f(x)$ into a rational inequality. Collecting terms over the common denominator $(x-1)(2x+3)$ produces a difference of two squares, which factorises into a product of two linear factors over a product of two linear factors. The four critical values split the line into five intervals, and a sign table decides each one. The subtlety is endpoint behaviour: where the numerator vanishes the inequality is satisfied, but where the denominator vanishes it is undefined, so two endpoints are included and two are excluded. The comparison also shows why the horizontal asymptotes are reciprocals rather than equal: the behaviour at large $x$ of $1/f$ is the reciprocal of the behaviour of $f$, so $y = 2$ becomes $y = 1/2$, while the two finite critical values simply exchange their roles as roots and poles.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.7 Solution of quadratic equations and inequalities and 2.6 The quadratic function
questions.question:
For each real number $k$, define $E(x)=(k+1)x^{2}-2(k+2)x+(k+5)$.

(a)

Show that the discriminant of $E(x)$ is equal to $-8k-4$.

[4]

(b)

Determine the set of values of $k$ for which $E(x)>0$ for every real number $x$.

[5]

(c)

Find the values of $x$ satisfying $E(x)>0$ when $k=-1$, where $E$ is no longer quadratic.

[3]

(d)

Determine the value of $k$ for which $E(x)=0$ has exactly one real solution, and state that solution.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Here $a=k+1$, $b=-2(k+2)$ and $c=k+5$, so the discriminant is $b^{2}-4ac$ (M1) $=4(k+2)^{2}-4(k+1)(k+5)$ (A1). Expanding, $(k+2)^{2}=k^{2}+4k+4$ and $(k+1)(k+5)=k^{2}+6k+5$ (A1), so the discriminant equals $4[(k^{2}+4k+4)-(k^{2}+6k+5)]=4(-2k-1)=-8k-4$ (A1) *(AG)*. The $k^{2}$ terms cancel, which is why the discriminant is linear in $k$ rather than quadratic, and this feature is what makes the later parts tractable.

(b) For $E(x)>0$ for every real $x$ the parabola must open upwards and have no real roots, so $a>0$ and the discriminant must be negative (M1). The discriminant $-8k-4$ is negative precisely when $-8k<4$, that is $k>-\frac{1}{2}$ (A1)(A1). For such values $k+1>\frac{1}{2}>0$, so the leading coefficient is automatically positive (R1), and the condition is exactly $k>-\frac{1}{2}$ (A1). No separate condition on $k$ is required beyond the discriminant inequality, because the boundary value of $k$ is greater than minus one and therefore keeps the leading coefficient positive.

(c) When $k=-1$ the coefficient of $x^{2}$ vanishes, so $E(x)=-2x+4$ (M1)(A1). Then $-2x+4>0$ gives $x<2$ (A1). The inequality is strict, so the endpoint $x=2$ is excluded and the solution set is the open ray to the left of two.

(d) A repeated root occurs when the discriminant is zero, so $-8k-4=0$ and $k=-\frac{1}{2}$ (M1)(A1). Substituting, $E(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x+\frac{9}{2}=\frac{1}{2}(x-3)^{2}$ (A1), so the single solution is $x=3$ (A1). The completed square shows that the expression is non-negative for every real $x$, and it is equal to zero only at the single point just found. The three answers form a consistent picture: below the boundary the expression is always positive, at the boundary it touches zero once, and beyond the boundary it changes sign.
questions.explanation:
The item is built around a single expression whose sign behaviour changes at two different parameter values. Part (a) is mechanical but sets up everything: the discriminant is linear in $k$, which is unusual for a quadratic family and is what makes the later parts tractable. Candidates who expect a quadratic discriminant and try to factor it waste time.

Part (b) is where the reasoning lives. The phrase 'for every real $x$' requires two separate conditions: the parabola must open upwards and must not touch the axis. Many candidates remember only the discriminant condition. Here the trap is benign, because the discriminant condition $k>-\frac{1}{2}$ already implies $k+1>0$, but the mark scheme rewards the candidate who notices this rather than one who assumes it. A candidate who writes $k>-\frac{1}{2}$ with no justification loses the reasoning mark.

Part (c) breaks the family. Setting $k=-1$ removes the quadratic term, and the expression becomes the decreasing line $-2x+4$. Candidates who blindly apply the discriminant to a line will divide by zero. This part exists to test whether the algebra is being watched.

Part (d) reuses the discriminant at its zero. The double root at $x=3$ is the natural bridge between the strict inequality of part (b) and the degenerate case of part (c). The classic errors are forgetting that $a>0$ is required in part (b); solving $-2x+4>0$ as $x>2$; and treating the repeated root as two coincident solutions. Plotting the family for a negative value of $k$ shows the parabola crossing the axis twice, which is precisely the case that the inequality in part (b) is designed to exclude. A useful sanity check is that the expression is a perfect square at the boundary, so its sign never becomes negative.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.10 Solving equations, both graphically and analytically and 2.9 Exponential functions and their graphs
questions.question:
Consider the function $f(x)=e^{2x}-5e^{x}+4$.

(a)

Show that the substitution $u=e^{x}$ reduces the equation $f(x)=0$ to $u^{2}-5u+4=0$, and hence solve $f(x)=0$ exactly.

[4]

(b)

Determine the set of values of $k$ for which $e^{2x}-5e^{x}+k=0$ has no real solutions.

[4]

(c)

Solve the inequality $f(x)>0$, giving your answer in exact form.

[4]

(d)

Determine the exact minimum value of $f(x)$ and the value of $x$ at which it occurs.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Since $e^{2x}=(e^{x})^{2}$, writing $u=e^{x}$ turns $f(x)=0$ into $u^{2}-5u+4=0$ (M1)(A1). Factorising, $(u-1)(u-4)=0$, so $u=1$ or $u=4$ (A1). Because $u=e^{x}$, this gives $e^{x}=1$ or $e^{x}=4$, that is $x=0$ or $x=\ln 4$ (A1). Both values of $u$ are positive, so both survive the substitution and give genuine real solutions for $x$.

(b) With $u=e^{x}>0$ the equation is $u^{2}-5u+k=0$ (M1). If the discriminant $25-4k$ is negative the quadratic has no real roots, so there is no positive $u$ and hence no real $x$ (A1)(M1). This requires $25-4k<0$, that is $k>\frac{25}{4}$ (A1). Conversely, for $k\le\frac{25}{4}$ the quadratic has at least one positive root, so real solutions exist; the answer is $k>\frac{25}{4}$. The converse direction is needed to show that no value of $k$ below the threshold can be added to the set.

(c) The inequality $f(x)>0$ becomes $u^{2}-5u+4>0$, that is $(u-1)(u-4)>0$ (M1)(A1), so $u<1$ or $u>4$ (A1). Translating back, $e^{x}<1$ or $e^{x}>4$, so $x<0$ or $x>\ln 4$ (A1). The two rays are disjoint, so the solution set is not an interval but the union of two separate pieces.

(d) Completing the square in $u$, $u^{2}-5u+4=\left(u-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{9}{4}$ (M1)(A1), so the least value is $-\frac{9}{4}$ (A1). This is attained when $u=\frac{5}{2}$, and since $\frac{5}{2}>0$ this corresponds to a real $x$ with $x=\ln\frac{5}{2}$ (A1). The positivity of the location is what guarantees that the stationary point of the quadratic is actually reached by the exponential curve, so the value is a true minimum rather than a lower bound.
questions.explanation:
This is the classic quadratic in disguise, but the question pushes past the standard version by asking for a parameter range and an exact minimum. The disguise is the point: $e^{2x}-5e^{x}+4$ looks like an exponential expression, yet the substitution $u=e^{x}$ makes it a quadratic. The whole question turns on remembering that $u$ is constrained to be positive.

Part (a) is routine once the substitution is seen. Part (b) is the subtle one. A candidate who requires only that the discriminant be negative obtains $k>\frac{25}{4}$ and is right, but for the wrong reason: they have not checked that the absence of real roots of the quadratic is enough. It is enough, because a negative discriminant means no real $u$ at all, positive or otherwise. The converse direction is what needs care, and the answer justifies it through the product of the roots.

Part (c) is a sign question. The factorisation $(u-1)(u-4)>0$ gives a union of two rays, not an interval. A candidate who writes $1<u<4$ has the sign backwards. Translating back to $x$ uses the fact that $e^{x}$ is increasing, so the inequalities are preserved.

Part (d) is an optimisation in the $u$-variable. The vertex of the quadratic is at $u=\frac{5}{2}$, which is positive, so the minimum of the quadratic is actually attained by the exponential function. This check is essential: had the vertex been at a negative value of $u$, the minimum of $f$ would not occur. A candidate who sketches the graph will see that the curve dips below the axis between the two roots and returns above it afterwards, which is exactly the sign pattern recorded in part (c). The value is attained, not merely approached, because the required value of the substituted variable is positive.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.11 Transformations of graphs
questions.question:
Let $f(x)=x^{2}-4x+5$.

(a)

Find $f(x)$ in the form $(x-h)^{2}+k$ and state the coordinates of the vertex of $y=f(x)$.

[4]

(b)

Describe the graph of $y=f(2x-6)$ as a combination of a horizontal stretch and a horizontal translation of the graph of $y=f(x)$, and explain why the translation is $6$ units in one order and $3$ units in the other.

[5]

(c)

Find the coordinates of the vertex of $y=f(2x-6)$.

[4]

(d)

Solve the equation $f(2x-6)=f(x)$, giving both solutions in exact form.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Completing the square, $f(x)=x^{2}-4x+4+1=(x-2)^{2}+1$ (M1)(A1). Comparing with $(x-h)^{2}+k$ gives $h=2$ and $k=1$ (A1), so the vertex is $(2,1)$ (A1). The completed-square form is the most convenient way to read off the vertex, and it will be reused in the later parts.

(b) Factorising the argument, $f(2x-6)=f(2(x-3))$ (M1). Starting from $y=f(x)$, a horizontal stretch of scale factor $\frac{1}{2}$ about the $y$-axis replaces $x$ by $2x$ and gives $y=f(2x)$ (A1), and translating the result $3$ units in the positive $x$-direction replaces $x$ by $x-3$, giving $y=f(2(x-3))=f(2x-6)$ (A1). In the other order, translating first by $6$ units gives $y=f(x-6)$ (M1), and then stretching by factor $\frac{1}{2}$ replaces $x$ by $2x$, giving $y=f(2x-6)$ (A1). The translation distances differ because the stretch acts on the translation itself: $2(x-3)=2x-6$, so a translation of $3$ before the stretch corresponds to a translation of $6$ after it. Both descriptions end at the same curve, and the discrepancy in the translation distance is the whole content of the part.

(c) Substituting into the completed-square form, $f(2x-6)=(2x-6-2)^{2}+1=(2x-8)^{2}+1=4(x-4)^{2}+1$ (M1)(A1). Hence the vertex is $(4,1)$ (A1)(A1). The vertex has the same height as before, which is expected because the stretch and the translation are both horizontal.

(d) Setting the two expressions equal, $4x^{2}-32x+65=x^{2}-4x+5$ (M1), so $3x^{2}-28x+60=0$ (A1). The quadratic formula gives $x=\frac{28\pm\sqrt{784-720}}{6}=\frac{28\pm8}{6}$ (A1), so the required solutions are $x=6$ or $x=\frac{10}{3}$. The two roots are the points at which the original parabola and its horizontally transformed copy have the same height. A quick check confirms that both values satisfy the simplified quadratic and that their sum and product match the coefficients.
questions.explanation:
The question looks like routine graph transformation, but the two orders in part (b) do not produce the same intermediate graph, and the reason is the whole point. A horizontal stretch by factor $\frac{1}{2}$ and a horizontal translation of $3$ units combine to give $f(2(x-3))$, whereas translating $6$ units first and then stretching gives the same final graph. The two descriptions are both correct because the stretch acts on whatever translation has already been applied.

The trap is to assume that transformations always commute. They do not: a horizontal translation and a horizontal stretch fail to commute unless the translation is zero. A candidate who writes 'stretch by $\frac{1}{2}$ then translate $6$' will produce the wrong intermediate expression, because the translation they have described belongs to the other stage. The mark scheme rewards the candidate who keeps the two orders separate and states the correct distance for each.

Part (c) is a straightforward substitution but is easy to get wrong if the completed-square form is not used. Expanding $f(2x-6)$ directly gives $4x^{2}-32x+65$, and completing the square on that expression is slower and more error-prone. Reading the vertex off the transformed form is the intended route.

Part (d) is an algebraic intersection problem. The two quadratics share the same $y$-intercept, which is why one root is far to the right and the other lies between $3$ and $4$. A candidate who tries to solve graphically without a calculator will struggle to locate $\frac{10}{3}$ precisely. The clean route is to cancel the $+1$ and take square roots, or to expand and use the formula, as shown. The base function was chosen so that both the vertex and the intersection points are simple fractions, which makes the transformation behaviour easy to check by hand.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 3.2 Sine, cosine and tangent ratios in right-angled triangles and 3.3 Applications of right and non-right angled trigonometry
questions.question:
In triangle $ABC$, the side $AB$ has length $6$ cm, the side $BC$ has length $2\sqrt{3}$ cm, and the angle $BAC$ is $30^{\circ}$. The remaining angles and sides are not yet known.

(a)

Show that there are two possible values of angle $BCA$, and find both of them.

[4]

(b)

Find the two possible values of angle $ABC$, giving each of them in degrees.

[4]

(c)

Find the two possible lengths of $CA$, giving each answer in the form $k\sqrt{3}$.

[4]

(d)

Determine the area of each triangle, and explain which one a student who assumes the triangle is right-angled would find.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) By the sine rule, $\frac{BC}{\sin BAC}=\frac{AB}{\sin BCA}$ (M1), so $\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{\sin 30^{\circ}}=\frac{6}{\sin BCA}$ (A1). Since $\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$, the left-hand side is $4\sqrt{3}$, giving $\sin BCA=\frac{6}{4\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (A1). Hence angle $BCA=60^{\circ}$ or $120^{\circ}$ (A1)(AG). Both values are admissible, because with angle $BAC=30^{\circ}$ each one leaves a positive third angle. The equation $\sin BCA=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is the crucial step, because the sine function takes the same value at two different angles in the range from $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$.

(b) The angle sum gives $ABC=180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}-BCA$ (M1). For $BCA=60^{\circ}$ this is $90^{\circ}$ (A1), and for $BCA=120^{\circ}$ it is $30^{\circ}$ (A1). Both values are positive, so both triangles exist (R1). The two third angles come from the same angle-sum relation, and neither is negative, which is the test that decides whether a candidate angle is admissible.

(c) Again by the sine rule, $\frac{CA}{\sin ABC}=4\sqrt{3}$ (M1), so $CA=4\sqrt{3}\sin ABC$ (A1). When $ABC=90^{\circ}$, $CA=4\sqrt{3}$ cm (A1); when $ABC=30^{\circ}$, $CA=4\sqrt{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=2\sqrt{3}$ cm (A1). The length of $CA$ depends on the angle opposite it, so the two possible values of angle $ABC$ produce two different lengths rather than one.

(d) The area is $\frac{1}{2}(AB)(BC)\sin ABC$ (M1) $=\frac{1}{2}(6)(2\sqrt{3})\sin ABC=6\sqrt{3}\sin ABC$ (A1). For $ABC=90^{\circ}$ this is $6\sqrt{3}$ cm$^{2}$ (A1), and for $ABC=30^{\circ}$ it is $6\sqrt{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=3\sqrt{3}$ cm$^{2}$ (A1). A candidate who assumes the triangle is right-angled obtains only the first value and never sees the obtuse case at all (R1). The area formula uses the two given sides and the angle between them, so it changes with the angle even though the sides themselves are fixed.
questions.explanation:
This item is built on the ambiguous case of the sine rule, and the ambiguity is genuine rather than decorative. The data are one side, a second side and a non-included angle, exactly the configuration in which two triangles can satisfy the same three measurements. The value $\sin BCA=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ has two solutions in the interval from $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$, namely $60^{\circ}$ and $120^{\circ}$, and both must be tested against the angle sum rather than discarded automatically.

The common error is to assume that the larger angle is impossible. Candidates who have memorised that a triangle cannot contain two obtuse angles sometimes reject $120^{\circ}$ without checking the sum. Here $30^{\circ}+120^{\circ}=150^{\circ}$, so the third angle is $30^{\circ}$ and the triangle is perfectly valid. The other error is the reverse: to accept only the acute solution because it is the one the calculator returns, since the inverse sine reports $60^{\circ}$ and hides $120^{\circ}$.

Part (d) gives the ambiguity a consequence. The two triangles have areas $6\sqrt{3}$ and $3\sqrt{3}$, and a candidate who silently assumes a right angle obtains only the larger one. The lever is therefore not the sine rule itself, which is routine, but the requirement to keep both branches alive through four linked parts and then to explain what is lost by collapsing them. The side $BC=2\sqrt{3}$ was chosen so that the sine-rule constant is the clean value $4\sqrt{3}$ and both lengths and both areas come out as exact multiples of $\sqrt{3}$. A sketch of both triangles, one with a right angle at $B$ and one with an obtuse angle at $C$, makes the two cases visually distinct. The final part asks what is lost when the right angle is assumed silently.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 3.3 Applications of right and non-right angled trigonometry
questions.question:
In triangle $PQR$, the side $PQ$ has length $7$ cm, the side $QR$ has length $15$ cm, and the area of the triangle is $42$ cm$^{2}$. A calculator is permitted throughout this question.

(a)

Show that $\sin Q=0.8$, and write down the two possible values of angle $PQR$ correct to one decimal place.

[4]

(b)

Find the two possible values of $PR$, giving one of them as an exact surd and one as an integer.

[5]

(c)

Determine the perimeter of each triangle, and state which of the two is obtuse-angled.

[4]

(d)

Explain why the area alone does not determine the triangle, and state one further measurement that would.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The area of a triangle is $\frac{1}{2}(PQ)(QR)\sin Q$ (M1), so $\frac{1}{2}(7)(15)\sin Q=42$ (A1). Since $\frac{1}{2}(7)(15)=52.5$, this gives $\sin Q=\frac{42}{52.5}=0.8$ (A1)(AG). Hence angle $PQR=53.1^{\circ}$ or $126.9^{\circ}$, correct to one decimal place (A1). The area formula is the only relation that uses the given quantity directly, and it is the reason the sine of the angle, rather than the angle itself, is what the data determine.

(b) By the cosine rule, $PR^{2}=PQ^{2}+QR^{2}-2(PQ)(QR)\cos Q$ (M1) $=7^{2}+15^{2}-210\cos Q=274-210\cos Q$ (A1). For $Q=53.1^{\circ}$ we have $\cos Q=0.6$, so $PR^{2}=274-126=148$ and $PR=2\sqrt{37}$ cm (M1)(A1). For $Q=126.9^{\circ}$ we have $\cos Q=-0.6$, so $PR^{2}=274+126=400$ and $PR=20$ cm (A1). The cosine rule is applied twice, once with the positive cosine and once with the negative, because the two cases differ only in the sign of $\cos Q$.

(c) The first perimeter is $7+15+2\sqrt{37}=34.2$ cm to three significant figures (M1)(A1). The second perimeter is $7+15+20=42$ cm (A1). The second triangle is obtuse-angled, because angle $PQR=126.9^{\circ}$ is greater than $90^{\circ}$ (R1). The perimeters differ by almost eight centimetres, which is a useful reminder that equal areas do not imply congruent triangles.

(d) The area fixes only $\sin Q$, and $\sin Q=\sin(180^{\circ}-Q)$, so an acute angle and its supplement produce the same area while giving two different triangles (M1)(A1). One further measurement would remove the ambiguity: whether angle $PQR$ is acute or obtuse, the length of $PR$, or the size of either of the remaining angles (A1). The ambiguity is a feature of the sine function rather than of the triangle, and it disappears as soon as any measurement that distinguishes an angle from its supplement is supplied.
questions.explanation:
The item is built around a quantity that is not determined by the information given. Two sides and the area fix $\sin Q$, but $\sin Q$ is the same for an acute angle and its supplement, so the data are consistent with two triangles of equal area. The cosine rule then separates them, because $\cos Q$ changes sign between the two cases: one triangle has $PR=2\sqrt{37}$, and the other has $PR=20$.

Candidates who use the cosine rule without thinking about the sign of $\cos Q$ will obtain only one value. If they assume the acute angle, they compute $274-126=148$; if they assume the obtuse angle, they compute $274+126=400$. Both are correct, but each belongs to a different triangle. The trap is to treat the second as an error rather than as the second branch.

Part (c) makes the distinction concrete through the perimeters, and the obtuse triangle is identified by the size of angle $Q$ rather than by any feature of the sides alone. Part (d) steps back and asks why the ambiguity arises in the first place; the answer is the symmetry $\sin Q=\sin(180^{\circ}-Q)$, which is also the reason the sine rule has an ambiguous case. The numbers $7$, $15$ and $42$ were chosen so that $\sin Q=0.8$ exactly and so that the two squared lengths are $148$ and $400$, the first reducing to $2\sqrt{37}$ and the second to a whole number. A candidate who checks $\cos^{2}Q+\sin^{2}Q=0.36+0.64=1$ will confirm that both branches correspond to genuine angles. The two triangles share the same two sides and the same area, so no measurement of area can ever separate them; only a measurement sensitive to the size of the angle can. It is the same ambiguity that appears in the ambiguous case of the sine rule.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.4 Linear correlation of bivariate data
questions.question:
Ten paired observations $(x,y)$ are summarised by $\sum x=60$, $\sum y=90$, $\sum x^{2}=400$, $\sum y^{2}=900$ and $\sum xy=588$.

(a)

Show that $S_{xx}=40$ and $S_{yy}=90$.

[4]

(b)

Calculate $S_{xy}$ and hence the product-moment correlation coefficient $r$.

[4]

(c)

Interpret $r$ in context, calculate the coefficient of determination, and comment on what it measures.

[4]

(d)

A student claims that because $r$ is close to $1$, an increase in $x$ causes an increase in $y$; explain why that conclusion does not follow from $r$.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The corrected sums are $S_{xx}=\sum x^{2}-\frac{(\sum x)^{2}}{n}=400-\frac{60^{2}}{10}$ (M1) $=400-360=40$ (A1). Similarly $S_{yy}=\sum y^{2}-\frac{(\sum y)^{2}}{n}=900-\frac{90^{2}}{10}$ (M1) $=900-810=90$ (A1)(AG). Both subtract the part of the sum of squares explained by the mean, leaving the variation about the mean.

(b) The cross term is $S_{xy}=\sum xy-\frac{(\sum x)(\sum y)}{n}=588-\frac{60\times 90}{10}$ (M1) $=588-540=48$ (A1). Hence $r=\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}=\frac{48}{\sqrt{40\times 90}}$ (M1) $=\frac{48}{\sqrt{3600}}=\frac{48}{60}=0.8$ (A1). The denominator is the geometric mean of the two variations, so $r$ measures the shared variation.

(c) The value $r=0.8$ indicates a strong positive linear relationship between $x$ and $y$, meaning that larger values of $x$ tend to accompany larger values of $y$ (A1). The coefficient of determination is $r^{2}=0.64$ (M1)(A1), so about $64$ per cent of the variation in $y$ is accounted for by the linear relationship with $x$. It measures the strength of the linear association only, not the agreement between the variables (R1). A high $r^{2}$ does not show that the linear model is the right one.

(d) A correlation coefficient measures association within the observed data and cannot establish direction or cause (M1). An increase in $y$ could cause an increase in $x$, or a third variable could drive both, so the relationship is symmetric in $x$ and $y$ and the roles can be exchanged without changing $r$ (A1)(A1). The correlation also depends on the range of values sampled and says nothing about values outside that range (R1). Causation requires additional evidence, such as a controlled experiment or a plausible mechanism.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the product-moment correlation coefficient and on what it does not license. The summary statistics are given in raw form, so the first task is to convert them into the corrected sums of squares. The sample size is ten, and the corrections subtract $\frac{60^{2}}{10}=360$ and $\frac{90^{2}}{10}=810$, leaving $S_{xx}=40$ and $S_{yy}=90$. These values are the variation about the mean in each variable, and the cross term $S_{xy}=48$ measures how much of that variation is shared.

The coefficient is then $\frac{48}{\sqrt{3600}}=\frac{48}{60}=0.8$, a value that most candidates will recognise as strong. The square, $0.64$, is the coefficient of determination and is the quantity that carries a percentage interpretation. The trap is the final part, where a student treats a large $r$ as evidence of cause. Correlation is symmetric: exchanging $x$ and $y$ leaves $r$ unchanged, so the data alone cannot tell which variable, if either, drives the other.

The common errors are to use $n-1$ in the correction term, which changes both $S_{xx}$ and $S_{yy}$ and destroys the exact value $0.8$, and to interpret $r^{2}$ as the proportion of points lying on the line. The numbers were chosen so that the denominator is exactly $60$ and the coefficient is exactly $0.8$, and so that the sample size is hidden inside the corrections rather than stated in the summaries. A candidate who notices that $r$ is unchanged when the roles of $x$ and $y$ are exchanged has the cleanest argument against causation.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.8 Binomial distribution
questions.question:
A trial has probability of success $p=0.3$ and is repeated $8$ times, with the trials independent of one another. A calculator is required throughout.

(a)

Find the probability that exactly $3$ of the $8$ trials succeed, giving your answer correct to six decimal places.

[4]

(b)

Find the probability that at least one of the $8$ trials succeeds.

[4]

(c)

Determine the smallest number of trials for which the probability of at least one success exceeds $0.99$.

[4]

(d)

Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the number of successes in $8$ trials.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) If $X$ denotes the number of successes then $X\sim B(8,0.3)$ (M1). The number of ways of choosing which three trials succeed is $\binom{8}{3}=56$ (A1), so $P(X=3)=56(0.3)^{3}(0.7)^{5}$ (M1) $=0.254122$ correct to six decimal places (A1). The coefficient counts the orders in which the three successes can appear, while the two powers record the probabilities of the successes and of the failures.

(b) The complement of at least one success is that no trial succeeds (M1), and $P(X=0)=(0.7)^{8}$ (A1). Therefore $P(X\ge 1)=1-(0.7)^{8}$ (A1) $=0.942352$ (A1). The complement rule replaces a sum of nine separate binomial terms by a single power, and it is correct because the events $X=0$ and $X\ge 1$ together exhaust the sample space.

(c) For $n$ trials the probability of at least one success is $1-(0.7)^{n}$ (M1), and this must exceed $0.99$, so $(0.7)^{n}<0.01$ (A1). Taking logarithms gives $n>\frac{\ln 0.01}{\ln 0.7}=12.91\ldots$ (M1), hence the smallest whole number of trials is $n=13$ (A1). The inequality reverses direction because $\ln 0.7$ is negative, and the value must be rounded up rather than to the nearest integer, since the inequality is strict.

(d) For a binomial distribution the mean is $np=8\times 0.3$ (M1) $=2.4$ (A1), and the variance is $np(1-p)=8\times 0.3\times 0.7=1.68$ (M1). The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so $\sqrt{1.68}=1.296148$ (A1). The mean is an expected count of successes while the standard deviation is measured in the same units as that count, so the two answers are consistent with each other and both describe the same binomial count.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the complement rule and on inverting the binomial inequality. Part (a) is a direct binomial probability and rewards candidates who can form the coefficient and the two powers. Part (b) is where the lever first appears: the phrase at least one invites a sum over eight or nine terms, but the complement reduces it to the single power $(0.7)^{8}$, and a candidate who does not see this will waste time or make an arithmetic slip.

Part (c) pushes the same idea further. The condition that the probability of at least one success exceeds $0.99$ becomes the inequality $(0.7)^{n}<0.01$, and solving it requires logarithms. The critical point is that $\ln 0.7$ is negative, so the inequality reverses when the logarithms are taken; a candidate who forgets this will obtain $n<12.91$ and answer $12$. Because $0.99$ is a strict threshold, the answer must be rounded up, and $12.91$ therefore gives $n=13$, not $12$.

Part (d) returns to the standard mean and variance formulae, $np$ and $np(1-p)$, and asks for the standard deviation rather than the variance, which catches candidates who stop one step early. The numbers $p=0.3$ and $n=8$ were chosen so that $(0.7)^{8}=0.942352$ and $(0.7)^{12}=0.986159$ fall just below $0.99$ while $(0.7)^{13}=0.990311$ rises above it, so the threshold genuinely separates consecutive trial counts. A candidate who treats the question as a single calculation, rather than as a search over whole numbers, will report $12.91$ and lose the final mark, because the question asks for a count of trials rather than for a boundary value.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.11 Formal definition and use of the formulae for conditional probability and independence
questions.question:
Items are produced either by machine $A$, with $P(A)=0.6$, or by machine $B$, with $P(B)=0.4$. The probability that an item is defective is $0.03$ given that it came from $A$ and $0.05$ given that it came from $B$. Let $D$ denote the event that an item is defective.

(a)

Find $P(D)$, the probability that a randomly chosen item is defective.

[4]

(b)

Given that an item is defective, find the probability that it came from machine $B$, giving your answer as an exact fraction.

[4]

(c)

Determine, showing your reasoning, whether the events 'from machine $A$' and 'defective' are independent.

[4]

(d)

The machines are adjusted so that $P(D\mid A)=P(D\mid B)=0.04$. Show that after the adjustment the events 'from machine $A$' and 'defective' are independent.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The law of total probability gives $P(D)=P(A)P(D\mid A)+P(B)P(D\mid B)$ (M1) $=0.6\times 0.03+0.4\times 0.05$ (A1) $=0.018+0.020=0.038$ (A1)(A1). The two machine cases are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so the overall defective rate is the weighted average of the two conditional rates, using the machine shares as weights, which is why the overall rate lies between the two conditional rates.

(b) Bayes' theorem gives $P(B\mid D)=\frac{P(B)P(D\mid B)}{P(D)}$ (M1) $=\frac{0.4\times 0.05}{0.038}$ (A1) $=\frac{0.020}{0.038}=\frac{20}{38}=\frac{10}{19}$ (A1). The conditioning is reversed here, so the numerator is the joint probability of $B$ and $D$, which is why the answer is not simply the given rate $0.05$ but the share of the defects attributable to machine $B$. This reversal of the conditioning is the whole content of Bayes' theorem.

(c) The events are independent exactly when $P(D\mid A)=P(D)$ (M1). Here $P(D\mid A)=0.03$ whereas $P(D)=0.038$ (A1), and these values are not equal (R1). Equivalently $P(A\cap D)=0.6\times 0.03=0.018$ while $P(A)P(D)=0.6\times 0.038=0.0228$ (A1), so the events are not independent when judged by the product of the marginal probabilities. Comparing the conditional rate with the overall rate is decisive because the two differ even though both numbers are small and both conditional rates lie close together.

(d) After the adjustment the overall rate is $P(D)=0.6\times 0.04+0.4\times 0.04=0.04$ (M1)(A1), while the conditional rate is $P(D\mid A)=0.04$ (A1). These are equal (R1)(AG). Because the conditional rate now coincides with the unconditional rate, knowing that an item came from machine $A$ gives no information about whether it is defective, so the two events are independent, and this remains true whatever the machine shares happen to be.
questions.explanation:
The item contrasts a conditional defective rate with an overall defective rate, and asks whether the machine and the defect are independent. Part (a) applies the law of total probability, giving $0.038$ as the weighted average of $0.03$ and $0.05$. Part (b) reverses the conditioning with Bayes' theorem and produces the exact fraction $\frac{10}{19}$. Both parts are standard, and they supply the numbers that the later parts need.

Part (c) is the lever. The events from machine $A$ and defective are independent exactly when $P(D\mid A)$ equals $P(D)$. Here the conditional rate is $0.03$ while the overall rate is $0.038$, so the events are dependent. Candidates frequently judge independence by looking at the two given conditional rates, $0.03$ and $0.05$, and concluding from their difference that the events must be dependent; this reasoning is not the definition, and it happens to give the wrong reason even when it gives the right verdict.

Part (d) removes the difference by setting both conditional rates to $0.04$. The overall rate then also becomes $0.04$, and the conditional and unconditional probabilities coincide, so the events become independent. The numbers were chosen so that the weighted average $0.038$ differs from both conditional rates and the fraction $\frac{10}{19}$ is exact, and so that the adjusted case gives the clean equality $0.04=0.04$. A candidate who reasons from the visible gap between $0.03$ and $0.05$ may reach the right verdict for the wrong reason, and part (d) is designed to expose that shortcut by removing the gap entirely.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.6 Derivative of x^n, sin x, cos x, e^x and ln x
questions.question:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^{4}\ln x$ for $x>0$.

(a)

By using the product rule on the two factors, show that $f'(x)=x^{3}(4\ln x+1)$.

[4]

(b)

Find the values of $f'(1)$ and $f'(e)$.

[4]

(c)

Determine the exact x-coordinate of the stationary point of $f$.

[4]

(d)

Find the value of $f$ at this stationary point.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) By the product rule, $f'(x)=4x^{3}\ln x+x^{4}\cdot\frac{1}{x}=4x^{3}\ln x+x^{3}=x^{3}(4\ln x+1)$ (M1)(A1)(A1)(AG). The derivative of $\ln x$ is $\frac{1}{x}$, which cancels one factor of $x$ in $x^{4}$ and leaves the $x^{3}$ term (R1). The factorised derivative is therefore confirmed as a product of $x^{3}$ and a logarithmic bracket. This structure is what makes the stationary point easy to locate once the factorisation is seen.

(b) At $x=1$, we have $\ln 1=0$, so $f'(1)=1^{3}(4\cdot0+1)=1$ (M1)(A1). At $x=e$, we have $\ln e=1$, so $f'(e)=e^{3}(4\cdot1+1)=5e^{3}$ (A1). The two gradient values are therefore $1$ and $5e^{3}$ (R1). The logarithm evaluates to $0$ at $1$ and to $1$ at $e$, which is exactly why these two inputs give such clean results.

(c) A stationary point satisfies $f'(x)=0$, so $x^{3}(4\ln x+1)=0$ (M1). Since the domain is $x>0$, the factor $x^{3}$ is never zero, leaving $4\ln x+1=0$, hence $\ln x=-\frac{1}{4}$ and $x=e^{-1/4}$ (A1)(A1). The coordinate is irrational because it is a non-integer power of $e$ (R1). The exact $x$-coordinate is therefore $e^{-1/4}$, a value that cannot be found by simple inspection.

(d) Substituting $x=e^{-1/4}$ gives $f(e^{-1/4})=(e^{-1/4})^{4}\ln(e^{-1/4})=e^{-1}\cdot(-\frac{1}{4})=-\frac{1}{4e}$ (M1)(A1), so the value is $-\frac{1}{4e}$ (A1). The power and the logarithm combine to produce a single negative fraction (R1). The value is therefore $-\frac{1}{4e}$, which is approximately $-0.09197$ and confirms the stationary point lies below the axis.
questions.explanation: This item combines the product rule with the derivative of $\ln x$ and then forces the candidate to solve for a stationary point that is not a nice rational number. The function $x^{4}\ln x$ differentiates, by the product rule, to $x^{3}(4\ln x+1)$, where the $1/x$ from $\ln x$ cancels one power of $x$. The intended route is to factor the derivative, evaluate it at $x=1$ and $x=e$ to get $1$ and $5e^{3}$, then set the derivative to zero; because $x^{3}$ is never zero for $x>0$, the stationary point comes from $4\ln x+1=0$, giving the irrational $x=e^{-1/4}$. The final value is $e^{-1}$ times $-1/4$, a negative fraction. The classic wrong turn is to mis-apply the product rule, writing $4x^{3}\ln x+4x^{3}$ or forgetting the $1/x$ factor, which destroys the factorisation. Candidates also try to factor out $x^{4}$ or to solve $x^{3}=0$ and claim a stationary point at $x=0$, ignoring the domain $x>0$. Another error is to evaluate $\ln(e^{-1/4})$ incorrectly, or to stop at $\ln x=-1/4$ without exponentiating to recover $x$. The numbers were chosen so that $x=1$ and $x=e$ give clean values and the stationary coordinate is a pure power of $e$, isolating the logarithm-solving skill as the genuine difficulty. The irrational answer is the feature that separates this item from a routine product-rule exercise, and the requirement to express the final value exactly as $-1/(4e)$ rather than as a rounded decimal is the final test of precision.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.9 Kinematic problems (displacement, velocity, acceleration)
questions.question:
A particle moves along a line with displacement $s(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$ metres at time $t$ seconds, for $t\ge 0$.

(a)

Show that the velocity is $v(t)=3(t-1)(t-3)$ and that the acceleration is $a(t)=6t-12$.

[4]

(b)

Find the times when the particle is at rest.

[4]

(c)

Find the displacement of the particle at those times.

[4]

(d)

Determine the total distance travelled by the particle in the interval $0\le t\le 4$.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Differentiate the displacement with respect to time to get the velocity $v(t)=3t^{2}-12t+9$ (M1), which factors as $3(t^{2}-4t+3)=3(t-1)(t-3)$ (A1)(AG). Differentiate once more to obtain the acceleration $a(t)=6t-12$ (A1). The velocity factorisation is exact, because expanding the bracket restores $3t^{2}-12t+9$, and this factored form makes the rest times immediate to read without solving a general quadratic.

(b) The particle is at rest when $v(t)=0$, so solve $3(t-1)(t-3)=0$ (M1). This gives $t-1=0$ or $t-3=0$, hence the two times $t=1$ and $t=3$ (A1). These are the only moments at which the velocity vanishes, so the direction of travel changes at both of these instants and the journey must be split there.

(c) Substitute each rest time into the displacement. At $t=1$ we have $s(1)=1-6+9=4$ (M1), and at $t=3$ we have $s(3)=27-54+27=0$ (A1). The displacements at the two stopping times are therefore $4$ m and $0$ m respectively, and the particle is momentarily stationary at each of these positions before it sets off again.

(d) Between $t=0$ and $t=4$ the particle moves from $s(0)=0$ out to $s(1)=4$, back to $s(3)=0$, then out again to $s(4)=4$ (M1). The three legs each have length $|4-0|=4$, $|0-4|=4$ and $|4-0|=4$ (A1), so the total distance is $4+4+4=12$ m (A1). Summing the absolute leg lengths is the only correct way to measure the path actually travelled, and the distinction between total distance and net displacement is the central idea tested here, so the total path length is the sum of three separate four-metre legs, which is why it equals $12$ and not the net displacement of $4$.
questions.explanation: The item is built on a kinematic cubic whose velocity has two distinct roots, so the particle stops and turns around twice within the interval. The displacement is $s(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$, whose derivative is $v(t)=3t^{2}-12t+9=3(t-1)(t-3)$, and the acceleration is $a(t)=6t-12$. The rest times are therefore $t=1$ and $t=3$, and the displacements there are $s(1)=4$ and $s(3)=0$. The trap, and the heart of the question, is that total distance is not the net displacement: between $t=0$ and $t=4$ the particle travels out to $4$, returns to $0$, and goes out again to $4$, so each leg is $4$ m and the total is $12$ m, whereas the net displacement from start to finish is only $4$ m. The intended route is to split the journey at the rest times, take the absolute value of each leg, and add them together. Splitting at the rest times is the only reliable way to capture the reversal, because a single displacement difference assumes monotonic motion throughout. The equal leg lengths are a direct consequence of the symmetric roots of the velocity, and they make the total distance an obvious multiple of one leg. The classic error is to compute $s(4)-s(0)=4$ and call that the distance travelled, which ignores the reversal completely. Another slip is to evaluate the acceleration at the rest times, $a(1)=-6$ and $a(3)=6$, and confuse its sign with the direction of motion. The numbers were chosen so the three legs are equal and integer, giving a clean total of $12$, while a candidate who omits the absolute values usually reports $4$ and fails the final part.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.10 Indefinite integral of x^n, sin x, cos x, 1/x, e^x
questions.question:
Find the indefinite integral $\int\left(3x^{2}-\frac{2}{x}+6\mathrm{e}^{x}-4\sin x\right)\mathrm{d}x$.

(a)

Find the general antiderivative, including the constant of integration.

[4]

(b)

Find the derivative of your answer and confirm that it returns the original integrand.

[4]

(c)

Find the value of the antiderivative at $x=1$, taking the constant of integration to be zero.

[4]

(d)

Find the constant of integration if the antiderivative takes the value $7$ when $x=1$.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Integrate the expression term by term, because the integral of a sum is the sum of the separate integrals. The power term gives $\int 3x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x=x^{3}$ (M1). The reciprocal term gives $\int -\frac{2}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=-2\ln|x|$ (A1), where the absolute value is required so the logarithm is defined. The exponential term gives $\int 6\mathrm{e}^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and the sine term gives $\int -4\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x=4\cos x$ (A1), since the derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$. No term affects another, so the four rules can be applied in any order, and adding the constant of integration gives the general antiderivative $F(x)=x^{3}-2\ln|x|+6\mathrm{e}^{x}+4\cos x+C$ (A1)(AG). Each standard rule is applied to one term independently, so the final result is the sum of four antiderivatives.

(b) Differentiate the answer to check it. We have $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x^{3})=3x^{2}$ (M1), $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(-2\ln|x|)=-\frac{2}{x}$ (A1), $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(6\mathrm{e}^{x})=6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(4\cos x)=-4\sin x$ (A1). Adding these derivatives gives exactly the original integrand $3x^{2}-\frac{2}{x}+6\mathrm{e}^{x}-4\sin x$ (A1)(AG). This reverse check is valuable, because it catches any single sign slip instantly, and the derivative undoes the integration term by term, which is why the check confirms the antiderivative is correct.

(c) With $C=0$ and $x=1$, substitute to obtain $F(1)=1-2\ln 1+6\mathrm{e}^{1}+4\cos 1$ (M1). Because $\ln 1=0$, this simplifies to $1+6\mathrm{e}+4\cos 1$, which evaluates to $19.470900$ to six decimal places (A1). The logarithm contributes nothing at $x=1$, so the value is dominated by the exponential and the cosine term, and those two terms together account for almost the whole magnitude of the result.

(d) The condition $F(1)=7$ gives $19.470900+C=7$ (M1), so the constant is $C=7-19.470900=-12.470900$ (A1)(AG). This constant shifts the whole antiderivative downwards so that its graph passes through the point $(1,7)$. Choosing the constant in this way fixes a unique member of the family of antiderivatives, and the negative sign is required because the value without the constant already exceeds $7$, which is why $C$ must be negative.
questions.explanation: The item is built on the indefinite integral of a sum that deliberately spans four different standard forms: a power, a reciprocal, an exponential and a sine. The antiderivative must combine a logarithm with a cosine, because integrating $-2/x$ gives $-2\ln|x|$ and integrating $-4\sin x$ gives $+4\cos x$, since the derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$. Combining a logarithm and a cosine in one antiderivative is unusual enough that candidates often second-guess the sign of the cosine term. The trap is to mishandle one of these signs, most often writing $-4\cos x$ instead of $+4\cos x$, or dropping the absolute value on the logarithm. Part (b) is the built-in self-check: differentiating the answer must return the integrand term by term, and it exposes any sign error at once. The evaluation at $x=1$ is chosen because $\ln 1$ vanishes, isolating the exponential and cosine contributions, so the value is $1+6\mathrm{e}+4\cos 1\approx 19.470900$. Part (d) then pins the curve by requiring $F(1)=7$, so $C=7-19.470900=-12.470900$, and requiring an initial condition turns the family of antiderivatives into a single curve. The classic error is to integrate $-4\sin x$ as $-4\cos x$, which fails the part (b) check, or to forget that $\ln 1=0$ and keep an erroneous constant term. The numbers were chosen so the part (c) value is not an integer, forcing a calculator evaluation, while the part (d) constant is a clean subtraction from it. The interplay of the four forms is the point of the exercise, and the logarithm-plus-cosine combination is the feature most likely to be mis-remembered under pressure. A calculator is genuinely needed only at the final numerical evaluation, since every algebraic step is exact.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.11 Definite integrals (areas between curves)
questions.question:
The region $R$ is bounded by the parabola $y=x^{2}-4$ and the line $y=2x-1$.

(a)

Find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the two curves intersect.

[4]

(b)

Show that the line $y=2x-1$ is the upper curve on the interval between the intersection points.

[4]

(c)

Find the total area enclosed by the two curves.

[4]

(d)

Find the area of the part of the region with $x\ge 0$.

[4]
questions.answer:
