(a) Set the two curves equal: $x^{2}-4=2x-1$ rearranges to $x^{2}-2x-3=0$ (M1). Factoring gives $(x-3)(x+1)=0$, so the intersection $x$-coordinates are $x=-1$ and $x=3$ (A1)(AG). Solving the quadratic is the necessary first step, because the limits of the area integral are exactly these $x$-values, and no other points bound the enclosed region between the two graphs.

(b) On the interval $[-1,3]$ compare the curves at a test point, for example $x=0$: the line gives $2(0)-1=-1$ while the parabola gives $0^{2}-4=-4$ (M1). Since $-1>-4$, the line lies above the parabola (A1). Equivalently the difference $(2x-1)-(x^{2}-4)=-x^{2}+2x+3=-(x-3)(x+1)$ is non-negative on $[-1,3]$ (A1)(AG). Confirming the upper curve matters, since integrating the lower minus the upper would give a negative result, and the non-negativity of the difference on the whole interval removes any doubt about which curve to subtract.

(c) The area is $\int_{-1}^{3}[(2x-1)-(x^{2}-4)]\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_{-1}^{3}(-x^{2}+2x+3)\,\mathrm{d}x$ (M1). The antiderivative is $-\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}+3x$ (A1), so evaluating gives $\left(-9+9+9\right)-\left(\frac{1}{3}+1-3\right)=9-\left(-\frac{5}{3}\right)=\frac{32}{3}$ (A1). The antiderivative is a simple cubic, so only arithmetic remains once the setup is correct, and the positive value confirms the orientation of the integration was chosen properly, which is why the answer is $\frac{32}{3}$.

(d) For the part with $x\ge 0$ the region runs from $0$ to $3$, so the area is $\int_{0}^{3}(-x^{2}+2x+3)\,\mathrm{d}x$ (M1). Using the same antiderivative gives $\left(-9+9+9\right)-0=9$ (A1)(AG). Restricting to $x$ at least zero simply changes the lower limit and leaves the integrand unchanged, and this sub-region is a clean integer, which makes the comparison with the full area instructive, so the area is exactly $9$ and not the full $\frac{32}{3}$.
questions.explanation: The item is built on the area between two curves, where the limits of integration come from the intersection of a parabola and a line. Setting $x^{2}-4=2x-1$ gives $x^{2}-2x-3=0$, which factors as $(x-3)(x+1)=0$, so the curves meet at $x=-1$ and $x=3$. The trap is to integrate the parabola minus the line, or to skip the check of which curve is on top; on $[-1,3]$ the line $y=2x-1$ lies above the parabola, because their difference $-x^{2}+2x+3=-(x-3)(x+1)$ is non-negative between the roots. The intended route is to integrate upper minus lower: $\int_{-1}^{3}(-x^{2}+2x+3)\,\mathrm{d}x$, whose antiderivative is $-\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}+3x$, giving $9-(-5/3)=32/3$. Part (d) then asks only for the right-hand portion with $x\ge 0$, which is $\int_{0}^{3}$ of the same integrand and equals $9$. Establishing the upper curve by the sign of the difference is the key step, because reversing the subtraction produces a negative area that no absolute value can later fix. The classic error is to use the wrong lower limit in part (d) by integrating from $-1$ to $0$, or to forget to subtract the antiderivative at the lower limit and write $9$ for the whole region instead of $32/3$. Another slip is to treat the two curves as if they cross again inside the interval. The numbers were chosen so the intersection roots are small integers and the two areas are the clean fractions $32/3$ and $9$, so a correct method produces exact values while a sign error does not. The clean integer sub-region makes the contrast with the full fractional area especially clear.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.15 Proof by mathematical induction
questions.question:
For each integer $n\ge1$, let $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{k^{2}+1}$.

(a)

Show that $\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}\le\dfrac{1}{k}-\dfrac{1}{k+1}$ for every integer $k\ge1$.

[3]

(b)

A student tries to prove by induction that $S_n<\dfrac32$ for all $n\ge1$. Explain why the inductive step cannot succeed when the hypothesis is only $S_k<\dfrac32$, writing down the strongest inequality that the step actually gives.

[4]

(c)

Prove by induction that $S_n\le\dfrac32-\dfrac1n$ for every integer $n\ge1$, and deduce that $S_n<\dfrac32$ for every integer $n\ge1$.

[5]

(d)

Determine the greatest real constant $c$ for which the inequality $S_n\le\dfrac32-\dfrac{c}{n}$ holds for every integer $n\ge1$, justifying your answer.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) For $k\ge1$,
$$\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{k+1}=\frac{(k+1)-k}{k(k+1)}=\frac{1}{k(k+1)}.$$ (M1) Now $(k+1)^{2}+1=k^{2}+2k+2$ and $k(k+1)=k^{2}+k$, so $$(k+1)^{2}+1-k(k+1)=k+2>0,$$ hence $(k+1)^{2}+1>k(k+1)$ and therefore $$\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}<\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}.$$ (A1)(A1) *(AG)*

(b) With the hypothesis $S_k<\frac32$ the step gives $$S_{k+1}=S_k+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}<\frac32+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}.$$ (M1)(A1) The right-hand side is strictly greater than $\frac32$ because $\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}>0$, so this does not establish $S_{k+1}<\frac32$. (R1) No rearrangement of a hypothesis of the form $S_k<\frac32$ can remove a positive increment, so the hypothesis has to be strengthened to one that leaves a gap larger than the increment. (A1)

(c) Claim: $S_n\le\frac32-\frac1n$ for all $n\ge1$. Base case $n=1$: $S_1=\frac12$ and $\frac32-1=\frac12$, so the claim holds, with equality. (M1) Inductive step: assume $S_k\le\frac32-\frac1k$. Then $$S_{k+1}=S_k+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}\le\frac32-\frac1k+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}.$$ (M1) By part (a), $\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}\le\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}$, so $$S_{k+1}\le\frac32-\frac1k+\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}=\frac32-\frac1{k+1}.$$ (A1) This is the claim with $n=k+1$, so by induction the claim holds for every $n\ge1$. (A1) *(AG)* Finally $\frac1n>0$, so $S_n\le\frac32-\frac1n<\frac32$ for every $n\ge1$. (A1)

(d) We want the largest $c$ with $S_n\le\frac32-\frac{c}{n}$ for all $n\ge1$. (M1) The case $n=1$ reads $\frac12\le\frac32-c$, that is $c\le1$, so no $c>1$ is admissible; part (c) shows that $c=1$ is admissible. (A1) Therefore the greatest such constant is $c=1$. (A1) For example, $c=\frac{3}{2}$ would demand $S_1\le0$, which is false because $S_1=\frac12$, so values above $1$ genuinely fail and the answer is not merely the largest value tested.
questions.explanation:
Part (a) is a small algebraic fact, but it is the engine of the whole question: it is exactly the telescoping difference $\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}$, which is slightly larger than the increment $\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}$. The denominator $k^{2}+1$ was chosen so that $(k+1)^{2}+1=k^{2}+2k+2$ exceeds $k(k+1)=k^{2}+k$ by exactly $k+2$, giving the clean comparison. Had the denominator been $k^{2}$, the comparison would point the wrong way and the argument would need a different tail entirely.

Part (b) is the conceptual heart. Induction is usually presented as 'assume it for $k$, prove it for $k+1$', and students expect the hypothesis to be used verbatim. Here the hypothesis $S_k<\frac32$ gives $S_{k+1}<\frac32+\frac{1}{(k+1)^{2}+1}$, a bound that has moved the wrong way. The bound is not merely inconvenient: because the increment is strictly positive, no amount of algebra starting from $S_k<\frac32$ can produce $S_{k+1}<\frac32$. The only way forward is to prove something stronger, a statement with a margin that grows and can therefore absorb the increment.

Part (c) supplies that margin. The tail $-\frac1n$ is chosen so that the slack between consecutive values, $\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}$, is at least the increment; part (a) is precisely that statement. The base case holds with equality and the step preserves the bound, so the stronger claim is established. Part (d) pins the constant: the base case forces $c\le1$, so $c=1$ is the best possible tail of this shape, and larger constants fail immediately at $n=1$.

The classic wrong turns are: assuming the hypothesis $S_k<\frac32$ is enough and writing a circular step; treating the inequality in (a) as an equality; trying to prove the weaker $S_n<2$ instead, which is true but does not answer the question; and in (d) forgetting that the base case, not the step, is what bounds $c$ from above. A useful check is that $S_1=\frac12$ exactly, which is why the constant $\frac32$ and the tail $\frac1n$ meet at $n=1$.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.12 Polynomial functions and equations; 2.14 Odd and even functions
questions.question:
The function $f$ is a cubic with leading coefficient $1$, and for all real $t$ it satisfies $$f(2+t)+f(2-t)=4.$$

(a)

Show that $g(t)=f(2+t)-2$ is an odd function, and deduce that $f(x)=2+a(x-2)^{3}+b(x-2)$ for some real constants $a$ and $b$.

[4]

(b)

Given also that $f$ has a repeated root, determine the values of $a$ and $b$ and hence the equation of $f(x)$.

[4]

(c)

Hence factorise $f(x)$ completely, state its roots, and determine the coordinates of its point of inflection.

[3]

(d)

Determine the number of real solutions of $f(x)=k$ for each real value of $k$, using the symmetry and the turning points of the graph.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Put $g(t)=f(2+t)-2$. Then $$g(t)+g(-t)=\bigl(f(2+t)-2\bigr)+\bigl(f(2-t)-2\bigr)=4-4=0,$$ (M1) using the given condition with the same $t$. Hence $g(-t)=-g(t)$ for all real $t$, so $g$ is odd. (A1)

Since $f$ is a cubic, $g$ is a cubic in $t$. An odd polynomial contains only odd powers of $t$, so $g(t)=at^{3}+bt$ for constants $a$ and $b$. (R1) Writing $t=x-2$ gives $f(x)-2=a(x-2)^{3}+b(x-2)$, that is $$f(x)=2+a(x-2)^{3}+b(x-2).$$ (A1) *(AG)*

(b) The leading coefficient of $f$ is $1$, so $a=1$. (A1) With $y=x-2$, the equation $f(x)=0$ becomes $$y^{3}+by+2=0.$$ (M1) A cubic $y^{3}+py+q$ has a repeated root exactly when its discriminant $-4p^{3}-27q^{2}$ is zero. (M1) Here $p=b$ and $q=2$, so $-4b^{3}-108=0$, giving $b^{3}=-27$ and hence $b=-3$. (A1) Therefore $$f(x)=(x-2)^{3}-3(x-2)+2.$$ (A1) *(AG)*

(c) Expanding, $(x-2)^{3}=x^{3}-6x^{2}+12x-8$ and $-3(x-2)=-3x+6$, so $$f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9x=x\left(x^{2}-6x+9\right)=x(x-3)^{2}.$$ (M1)(A1) The roots are $x=0$ and the repeated root $x=3$. (A1) The point of inflection is the centre of symmetry $(2,2)$, since $f(2)=2$; equivalently $f''(x)=6x-12$ vanishes at $x=2$. (A1) As a check on the symmetry, the half-turn about $(2,2)$ carries the point $(0,0)$ to $(4,4)$, and indeed $f(4)=4$.

(d) Differentiating, $f'(x)=3x^{2}-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)$. (M1) Hence $f$ has a local maximum at $x=1$ with $f(1)=4$ and a local minimum at $x=3$ with $f(3)=0$. (A1) These are reflections of each other in the point of symmetry $(2,2)$, since $2\cdot2-1=3$ and $2\cdot2-4=0$. (A1) Reading the graph: for $k<0$ there is one solution; for $k=0$ there are two distinct solutions, $x=0$ and the repeated root $x=3$; for $0<k<4$ there are three solutions; for $k=4$ there are two distinct solutions; and for $k>4$ there is one solution. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The stem states the symmetry as a functional equation about the point $(2,2)$, not about the origin, and this is the whole difficulty. An even function satisfies $h(-x)=h(x)$ and an odd function satisfies $h(-x)=-h(x)$, but neither applies to $f$ directly. Subtracting the centre, $g(t)=f(2+t)-2$, moves the point of symmetry to the origin, and only then does the odd condition become usable. This construction is the step students skip: they look for odd or even powers of $x$ in $f$ and find none, because the symmetry lives in the translated variable $x-2$.

Once $g$ is known to be odd, the shape of $f$ is forced: a polynomial odd in $t$ has only odd powers, so $f(x)=2+a(x-2)^{3}+b(x-2)$. Part (b) then pins the coefficients. The leading coefficient fixes $a=1$, and the repeated root fixes $b$. The clean way to use the repeated root is the discriminant: after the substitution $y=x-2$, the equation is $y^{3}+by+2=0$, and its discriminant $-4b^{3}-108$ vanishes only at $b=-3$. There is no second value, so the cubic is unique.

Part (c) reveals why the numbers were chosen: the cubic factors as $x(x-3)^{2}$, so the repeated root sits at $x=3$ and the simple root at $x=0$, both consistent with the central symmetry about $(2,2)$, which swaps the point $(1,4)$ with $(3,0)$.

Part (d) is where the graph features matter. The local maximum and minimum are images of each other under the half-turn about $(2,2)$, so the horizontal lines $y=k$ cut the graph in a pattern symmetric about $k=2$. The subtle cases are $k=0$ and $k=4$, where the line passes through a turning point and the double root means only two distinct solutions. The classic wrong turns are treating the symmetry as being about $x=0$, forgetting that the repeated root gives a double but not a triple solution, and missing the degenerate counts at the turning-point values.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 3.10 Compound angle identities; 3.11 Relationships between trigonometric functions
questions.question:
Consider the equation $$\cos 2x=\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right).$$

(a)

Show that $\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\cos x-\sin x$ and that $\cos 2x=(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x)$.

[3]

(b)

Hence solve the equation $\cos 2x=\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ for $0\le x<2\pi$, giving each answer as a multiple of $\pi$.

[4]

(c)

A student solves the equation by squaring both sides. Explain how this leads to $\sin 2x(\sin 2x-1)=0$, and identify the extraneous solutions that the squaring introduces.

[4]

(d)

Determine the general solution of the equation, and hence the number of solutions that lie in the interval $-2\pi\le x\le2\pi$.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) By the compound-angle formula, $$\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sqrt2\left(\cos x\cos\frac{\pi}{4}-\sin x\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sqrt2\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}(\cos x-\sin x)=\cos x-\sin x.$$ (M1)(A1) Also, by the double-angle formula and the difference of two squares, $$\cos 2x=\cos^{2}x-\sin^{2}x=(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x).$$ (A1) *(AG)*

(b) Substituting the results of (a), $$(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x)=\cos x-\sin x,$$ so $$(\cos x-\sin x)\bigl(\cos x+\sin x-1\bigr)=0.$$ (M1)

Case 1: $\cos x=\sin x$, that is $\tan x=1$, giving $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ or $x=\frac{5\pi}{4}$ in $[0,2\pi)$. (A1)

Case 2: $\cos x+\sin x=1$. Writing the left side as $\sqrt2\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ gives $\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $x-\frac{\pi}{4}=\pm\frac{\pi}{4}+2k\pi$. (M1) Hence $x=0$ or $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ in $[0,2\pi)$. (A1)

The solutions are $x=0$, $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$, $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi}{4}$.

(c) Squaring both sides gives $\cos^{2}2x=2\cos^{2}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$. (M1) Using $\cos^{2}2x=1-\sin^{2}2x$ and $2\cos^{2}\theta=1+\cos2\theta$ with $\theta=x+\frac{\pi}{4}$, the right-hand side is $$1+\cos\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=1-\sin2x.$$ (A1) Hence $1-\sin^{2}2x=1-\sin2x$, that is $\sin^{2}2x=\sin2x$, or $$\sin2x\,(\sin2x-1)=0.$$ (A1)

The squared equation therefore admits $x=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2}$ from $\sin2x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}$ from $\sin2x=1$. (A1) Of these, $x=\pi$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ do not solve the original equation: at $x=\pi$ the left side is $1$ and the right side is $-1$, while at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ the left side is $-1$ and the right side is $1$. They are extraneous and must be rejected.

(d) From (b), $\cos x=\sin x$ gives $x=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi$ for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. (M1) Also $\cos x+\sin x=1$ gives $x=2k\pi$ or $x=\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi$ for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. (A1)

In $[-2\pi,2\pi]$ the family $\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi$ contributes $k=-2,-1,0,1$, that is $-\frac{7\pi}{4},-\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}$, four values; the family $2k\pi$ contributes $-2\pi,0,2\pi$, three values; and the family $\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi$ contributes $-\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}$, two values. (M1) These nine values are all distinct, so there are $9$ solutions. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The equation is dressed in a compound angle, and the first move is to expand $\sqrt2\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ with the compound-angle identity. That expansion is not cosmetic: it produces $\cos x-\sin x$, which is exactly the factor that $\cos2x$ contains by the difference of two squares. The whole equation therefore becomes $(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x)=(\cos x-\sin x)$, and factorising reduces it to two simple cases. This is the structural reason that $\sqrt2$ and $\frac{\pi}{4}$ appear together: they are chosen so that the compound-angle expansion matches the double-angle factorisation.

The first trap is the common factor $\cos x-\sin x$. Dividing by it discards the two solutions where it vanishes, $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi}{4}$. Factorising keeps them. This is the standard error in this family of equations, and part (b) is arranged so that a careless cancellation still yields two of the four answers, which makes the mistake easy to miss.

Part (c) exposes a second trap, squaring. Squaring both sides is superficially attractive because both $\cos2x$ and $\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ invite a double-angle identity. It does give a solvable equation, $\sin2x(\sin2x-1)=0$, but squaring is not reversible and enlarges the solution set. The two values $x=\pi$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ solve the squared equation because the two sides have equal magnitude there but opposite signs, so the residual is $\pm2$ rather than $0$. Identifying and testing these is the point of the part.

Part (d) asks for the general solution and then counts over a closed interval of length $4\pi$. The three families $\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi$, $2k\pi$ and $\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi$ must each be enumerated; both endpoints $x=\pm2\pi$ belong to the second family, so omitting either loses a solution. The classic wrong turns are cancelling the common factor, accepting the roots introduced by squaring, and forgetting either the parameter $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ or the closed endpoints.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 3.9 Reciprocal trigonometric ratios sec, csc and cot
questions.question:
For real $x$ where it is defined, let $$f(x)=\csc x-\cot x.$$

(a)

State the values of $x$ in the interval $[0,2\pi)$ at which $f(x)$ is undefined, and write down the period of $f$.

[3]

(b)

Show that $f(x)=\tan\dfrac{x}{2}$ for every $x$ in the domain of $f$.

[4]

(c)

A student solves $f(x)=1$ by multiplying both sides by $\sin x$. Show that this produces the equation $\sin x+\cos x=1$, and hence find all solutions of that produced equation in $[0,2\pi)$.

[4]

(d)

Determine the number of solutions of $f(x)=k$ in $[0,2\pi)$ for $k>0$, for $k=0$ and for $k<0$, justifying your answers by reference to the graph of $f$.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) $f$ is undefined where $\sin x=0$, because $\csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x}$ and $\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ both require $\sin x\ne0$. (A1) In $[0,2\pi)$ these are $x=0$ and $x=\pi$. (A1) Both reciprocal functions have period $2\pi$, so $f$ has period $2\pi$. (A1)

(b) Putting the two terms over the common denominator, $$\csc x-\cot x=\frac{1}{\sin x}-\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\frac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}.$$ (M1) The half-angle identity $\tan\frac{x}{2}=\frac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}$ holds for every $x$ with $\sin x\ne0$. (M1) Hence $f(x)=\tan\frac{x}{2}$ on the whole domain of $f$. (A1) *(AG)*

(c) Multiplying $f(x)=1$ by $\sin x$ gives $1-\cos x=\sin x$, that is $$\sin x+\cos x=1.$$ (M1)(A1) Writing the left side as $\sqrt2\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ gives $\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $x+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{4}$ or $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ in the first period. (M1) The solutions in $[0,2\pi)$ are $x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$. (A1) At $x=0$, however, $\sin x=0$, so $f$ is undefined and the multiplication by zero has created a false root; only $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ solves the original equation. (R1)(A1)

(d) On the domain $f(x)=\tan\frac{x}{2}$ with $\frac{x}{2}\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\cup\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)$. (M1) On $\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ the tangent rises from $0$ to $+\infty$, so each $k>0$ is attained exactly once and no $k<0$ is attained. (A1) On $\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)$ it rises from $-\infty$ to $0$, so each $k<0$ is attained exactly once and no $k>0$ is attained. (A1) For $k=0$, $\tan\frac{x}{2}=0$ would require $x=0$ or $x=2\pi$, both excluded, so there are no solutions. (R1) Hence $f(x)=k$ has exactly one solution for every $k\ne0$ and none for $k=0$. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The stem is deliberately bare: the difficulty lies not in the algebra but in noticing where the algebra is legal. The reciprocal functions are defined by $\csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x}$ and $\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$, so both fail wherever $\sin x=0$. On $[0,2\pi)$ that is exactly $x=0$ and $x=\pi$, and every later part is governed by those two points.

Part (b) is the structural key. The combination $\csc x-\cot x$ collapses to $\frac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}$, which is precisely the half-angle expression for $\tan\frac{x}{2}$. Two reciprocal functions that look like a hard mixture are secretly a single tangent, and this turns the equation into a monotonic one.

Part (c) is where the trap bites. Multiplying by $\sin x$ clears the denominator and gives the clean equation $\sin x+\cos x=1$, whose solutions in the interval are $x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$. But the multiplication is not reversible at $x=0$, where $\sin x=0$: it multiplies by zero and manufactures a root the original equation never had, because $f$ is not even defined there. Each root must be tested against the domain.

Part (d) uses the reduced form as a graph. The domain splits into two open intervals, and on each the half-angle runs through a half-period of the tangent, so the branches together cover every nonzero real value exactly once and never cover zero. For $k=0$ the algebra suggests $x=0$ and $x=2\pi$, but both are excluded, so there are no solutions. The classic errors are accepting $x=0$ in (c), forgetting the excluded point $x=\pi$, and claiming two solutions for every $k$ by ignoring the split domain. A candidate who trusts the multiplied equation will report two answers where only one is genuine.

questions.subtopic: 5.12 Continuity and differentiability; 5.15 Further derivatives
questions.question:
Let $a>0$ with $a\ne1$, and let $p,q,r,s,t$ be real constants. Define $$f(x)=\begin{cases} a^{x}+\log_a x+p, & 0<x\le1,\\[4pt] q\tan(x-1)+r, & 1<x\le1+\frac{\pi}{4},\\[4pt] s\csc(x-1)+t, & 1+\frac{\pi}{4}<x<1+\pi. \end{cases}$$

(a)

Show that $f$ is continuous at $x=1$ exactly when $a+p=r$, and that $f$ is continuous at $x=1+\frac{\pi}{4}$ exactly when $q+r=s\sqrt2+t$.

[4]

(b)

By differentiating each branch, show that $f$ is differentiable at $x=1$ exactly when $a+p=r$ and $q=a\ln a+\frac{1}{\ln a}$, and that $f$ is differentiable at $x=1+\frac{\pi}{4}$ exactly when $q+r=s\sqrt2+t$ and $s=-\sqrt2\,q$.

[4]

(c)

Determine all parameter choices for which $f$ is continuous at $x=1$ but not differentiable there, and explain why no choice of parameters makes $f$ differentiable at $x=1$ while failing to be continuous there.

[4]

(d)

Taking $a=e$ and $r=0$, determine the coordinates of the stationary point of $f$ on the third branch when $f$ is differentiable at both joins, and justify that this point is a local maximum.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) At $x=1$ the left limit is $a^{1}+\log_a1+p=a+p$, while the right-hand value is $q\tan0+r=r$. (M1)(A1) These agree exactly when $a+p=r$. (AG) At $x=1+\frac{\pi}{4}$ the left limit is $q\tan\frac{\pi}{4}+r=q+r$ and the right-hand value is $s\csc\frac{\pi}{4}+t=s\sqrt2+t$; these agree exactly when $q+r=s\sqrt2+t$. (M1)(A1) *(AG)*

(b) The first branch has derivative $a^{x}\ln a+\frac{1}{x\ln a}$, equal at $x=1$ to $a\ln a+\frac{1}{\ln a}$; the second has derivative $q\sec^{2}(x-1)$, equal at $x=1$ to $q$. (M1)(A1) Differentiability at $x=1$ needs continuity and equality of these one-sided derivatives, giving $a+p=r$ and $q=a\ln a+\frac{1}{\ln a}$. (A1) At $x=1+\frac{\pi}{4}$ the second branch has derivative $q\sec^{2}\frac{\pi}{4}=2q$, and the third has derivative $-s\csc(x-1)\cot(x-1)$, equal there to $-s\sqrt2$. (M1) So differentiability at that join requires $q+r=s\sqrt2+t$ together with $2q=-s\sqrt2$, that is $s=-\sqrt2\,q$. (A1) *(AG)*

(c) Continuity at $x=1$ is the single condition $a+p=r$; differentiability adds the independent condition $q=a\ln a+\frac{1}{\ln a}$. (M1) Hence $f$ is continuous but not differentiable at $x=1$ precisely when $a+p=r$ and $q\ne a\ln a+\frac{1}{\ln a}$, for any admissible $a$. (A1) The reverse cannot occur: a function differentiable at a point must be continuous there, since a differentiable function has a tangent line and cannot break. (R1)(A1)

(d) With $a=e$ we have $\ln a=1$, so $q=e+1$, then $s=-\sqrt2(e+1)$ and $t=q+r-s\sqrt2=3(e+1)$. (M1) On the third branch $f'(x)=-s\csc(x-1)\cot(x-1)=\sqrt2(e+1)\csc(x-1)\cot(x-1)$, which vanishes when $\cot(x-1)=0$, that is at $x=1+\frac{\pi}{2}$. (A1) There $f=s\csc\frac{\pi}{2}+t=s+t=(3-\sqrt2)(e+1)$, so the stationary point is $\left(1+\frac{\pi}{2},\,(3-\sqrt2)(e+1)\right)$. Since $f'$ is positive just left of $x=1+\frac{\pi}{2}$ and negative just right, the point is a local maximum. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The function is assembled so that each branch forces a different derivative rule, and so that the two conditions imposed at each join are logically independent. That independence is the point: continuity and differentiability are often conflated, and here they are made to disagree in a visible, parameterised way.

At $x=1$ the left branch $a^{x}+\log_a x+p$ contributes the rules $\frac{d}{dx}a^{x}=a^{x}\ln a$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\log_a x=\frac{1}{x\ln a}$, so its slope is $a\ln a+\frac{1}{\ln a}$, while the right branch $q\tan(x-1)+r$ has slope $q$. Continuity matches the values and gives $a+p=r$; differentiability additionally matches the slopes and gives the second, independent condition. No value condition can produce a slope condition, so for a whole family of parameters the graph is continuous at $x=1$ yet has a corner there. This is exactly the informal relationship the syllabus describes: continuity is necessary for differentiability but not sufficient.

The second join repeats the pattern with the reciprocal functions. Differentiating $q\tan(x-1)$ at $x=1+\frac{\pi}{4}$ uses $\sec^{2}$, giving $2q$, while differentiating $s\csc(x-1)$ uses $-\csc\cot$, giving $-s\sqrt2$; equality of slopes then fixes $s$ in terms of $q$, and continuity fixes $t$. Because $\sec^{2}$ and $-\csc\cot$ are genuinely different, the two joins do not merely repeat one calculation.

Part (d) tests whether the parameter relations can be carried through to a concrete graph. With $a=e$ the logarithm becomes natural, $q=e+1$, and the third branch has a stationary point where $\cot(x-1)=0$. The classic wrong turns are equating values instead of slopes, forgetting that differentiability requires continuity, differentiating $\log_a x$ as $\frac{1}{x}$, and losing the factor $\sqrt2$ from $\csc\frac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.6 Simple deductive proof, numerical and algebraic
questions.question:
The task is to prove that there are no positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfying the equation $a^{2} + b^{2} = 3c^{2}$.

(a)

Show that the square of every integer leaves remainder $0$ or $1$ when divided by $3$.

[3]

(b)

Deduce that if $a^{2} + b^{2} = 3c^{2}$ for integers $a$, $b$ and $c$, then $3$ divides both $a$ and $b$.

[4]

(c)

Hence show that there are no positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ with $a^{2} + b^{2} = 3c^{2}$.

[5]

(d)

Explain why the same argument with $3$ replaced by $2$ does not force $a$ and $b$ to be even, and give a solution of $a^{2} + b^{2} = 2c^{2}$ showing that the corresponding conclusion is false.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Every integer is of the form $3k$, $3k+1$ or $3k+2$. (M1) Squaring these gives $9k^{2}$, $9k^{2} + 6k + 1$ and $9k^{2} + 12k + 4$. (M1) The first is divisible by $3$, while the second and third leave remainder $1$, so every square leaves remainder $0$ or $1$. (A1)

(b) By part (a), $a^{2}$ and $b^{2}$ each leave remainder $0$ or $1$ modulo $3$, so $a^{2} + b^{2}$ leaves remainder $0$, $1$ or $2$. (M1) The right-hand side $3c^{2}$ is divisible by $3$, so the left-hand side must leave remainder $0$. (M1) Remainder $0$ forces $0 + 0$, so $a^{2}$ and $b^{2}$ are both divisible by $3$. (A1) A square divisible by $3$ forces its root to be divisible by $3$, so $3 \mid a$ and $3 \mid b$. (A1)

(c) From part (b), write $a = 3a_1$ and $b = 3b_1$. (M1) Substituting gives $9a_1^{2} + 9b_1^{2} = 3c^{2}$, so $3(a_1^{2} + b_1^{2}) = c^{2}$. (M1) Therefore $3 \mid c^{2}$ and hence $3 \mid c$. (A1) Writing $c = 3c_1$ and dividing by $3$ gives $a_1^{2} + b_1^{2} = 3c_1^{2}$. (M1) So $(a_1, b_1, c_1)$ is another positive integer solution with $a_1 < a$. (A1) Repeating without end produces a strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, which is impossible, so no such triple exists. (R1)

(d) Modulo $2$, every square leaves remainder $0$ or $1$. (M1) Both $0 + 0$ and $1 + 1$ leave remainder $0$ modulo $2$, so the congruence does not force $a$ and $b$ even. (A1) Indeed $a = b = c = 1$ gives $1 + 1 = 2 = 2 \times 1$, a genuine solution. (R1)
questions.explanation:
This is a proof by infinite descent, and the whole argument hinges on the modulus being three. Modulo $3$ the squares are only $0$ and $1$, so a sum of two squares can take remainder $0$, $1$ or $2$. The right-hand side $3c^{2}$ is always divisible by $3$, so the remainder must be $0$, and the only way two residues drawn from $0$ and $1$ sum to $0$ modulo $3$ is $0 + 0$. Both $a^{2}$ and $b^{2}$ are therefore divisible by $3$, which forces both $a$ and $b$ to be divisible by $3$.

Part (c) turns this into a descent. Writing $a = 3a_1$ and $b = 3b_1$ and substituting gives $c^{2} = 3(a_1^{2} + b_1^{2})$, so $c$ is also divisible by $3$. Dividing through by $3$ produces a smaller solution $(a_1, b_1, c_1)$ of the same equation. If a solution existed, this process could be repeated without end, generating a strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, and no such sequence can exist. That contradiction proves the equation has no positive integer solutions.

Part (d) is the discriminating step. The same style of argument with $3$ replaced by $2$ fails, because modulo $2$ the squares are again $0$ and $1$ but now $1 + 1$ is also congruent to $0$, just as $0 + 0$ is. The congruence therefore does not force $a$ and $b$ to be even, and indeed $a = b = c = 1$ satisfies $a^{2} + b^{2} = 2c^{2}$. The classic errors are asserting $3 \mid a$ without justifying that a square divisible by $3$ forces its root to be divisible by $3$, and stopping the descent after one step without naming the impossibility.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.13 Bayes' theorem
questions.question:
A component is selected at random from a day's output.

(a)

Find the probability that the component is defective.

[4]

(b)

Given that the component is defective, determine the probability that it was made by machine $M_{2}$.

[4]

(c)

Components are packed in boxes of 20. Find the probability that a box contains at least one defective component.

[4]

(d)

A quality-control inspector tests components one at a time until a defective one is found. Given that the fifth component tested is the first defective one, find the probability that it was made by machine $M_{3}$, and explain why the answer is the same as if the first component tested had been defective.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Let $D$ be the event 'defective'.

$$P(D)=P(M_{1})P(D\mid M_{1})+P(M_{2})P(D\mid M_{2})+P(M_{3})P(D\mid M_{3})$$ (M1)

$$=0.40(0.02)+0.35(0.03)+0.25(0.05)$$ (A1)

$$=0.008+0.0105+0.0125$$ (A1)

$$P(D)=0.031\ \ (3.1\%).$$ (A1)

(b) By Bayes' theorem:

$$P(M_{2}\mid D)=\frac{P(M_{2}\cap D)}{P(D)}=\frac{P(M_{2})P(D\mid M_{2})}{P(D)}$$ (M1)

$$=\frac{0.35(0.03)}{0.031}=\frac{0.0105}{0.031}$$ (A1)

$$=0.3387\ldots$$ (A1)

$$P(M_{2}\mid D)=0.339\ (3\ \text{s.f.})$$ (A1)

(c) Let $X$ be the number of defectives in a box. Then $X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,\,0.031)$. (M1)(A1)

$$P(X\ge1)=1-P(X=0)=1-(1-0.031)^{20}$$ (M1)

$$=1-0.969^{20}=1-0.5326$$ (A1)

$$=0.467\ (3\ \text{s.f.})$$

(d) The fifth component tested is defective, and components 1 to 4 are not. Let $F$ be this event.

$$P(M_{3}\mid F)=\frac{P(M_{3}\cap F)}{P(F)}=\frac{P(M_{3}\cap D)}{P(D)}$$ (M1)(A1)

because $F$ says exactly two things about component 5 — that it is defective, and that components 1–4 are not — and the machine that made component 5 is independent of what was found in components 1–4. So the information about components 1–4 is irrelevant to the question asked, and $F$ reduces to '$D$' for the fifth component.

$$=\frac{0.25(0.05)}{0.031}=\frac{0.0125}{0.031}=0.4032\ldots$$ (A1)

$$P(M_{3}\mid F)=0.403\ (3\ \text{s.f.})$$

Why it is the same as for the first component: whether the defective component turns up first, fifth or fiftieth, the only fact that carries information about its origin is that it *is* defective. The positions of the earlier non-defective components depend on the overall defective rate $P(D)=0.031$, which is the same for every machine's output because the components are mixed before packing; they therefore tell us nothing new about which machine made the one we eventually found. (R1)
questions.explanation:
Parts (a)–(c) are a conventional Bayes-and-binomial exercise. Part (d) is the question.

On seeing 'the fifth component tested is the first defective one', most candidates reach for a geometric distribution and start computing $(0.969)^{4}(0.031)$. That calculation is not wrong, but it is unnecessary: the factor $0.969^{4}$ appears in both the numerator and the denominator and cancels. What survives is exactly the answer to (b)-style question for $M_3$.

The reason is structural, and it is what the question is testing. The components are mixed before packing, so the machine that made any given component is independent of the machine that made any other. Learning that components 1–4 were *not* defective tells you something about the overall defective rate — but that rate is already known ($0.031$) and is the same whichever machine made component 5. So the extra information is genuinely irrelevant to the question asked.

This is the same reason a gambler's 'the roulette wheel hasn't landed on red for ten spins, so red is due' reasoning fails — and it is worth saying out loud in class after marking this.

Classic wrong turns: answering $P(M_3)=0.25$ (ignoring the conditioning entirely); using $P(D\mid M_3)=0.05$ as the answer; and, most commonly, computing the full geometric expression in (d), getting the right number, and then being unable to say *why* the 5 is irrelevant — which forfeits the reasoning mark.

Two further wrong turns belong to part (c). The first is to add the twenty individual defect probabilities and answer $20\times0.031=0.62$; the events overlap, so the complement $1-P(\text{none defective})$ is the correct route. The second is to run the binomial with $p=0.05$, the rate of $M_{3}$, rather than the pooled rate $0.031$; the box is filled from the mixed output of all three machines.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.14 Complex conjugate roots of polynomial equations
questions.question:
Let $P(z)=z^{3}+pz^{2}+qz+r$, where $p$, $q$ and $r$ are real numbers.

(a)

Explain why, if $z_{0}$ is a non-real root of $P$, then $\bar z_{0}$ is also a root of $P$, and deduce that $P$ has exactly one real root.

[3]

(b)

Suppose $P$ has a root of the form $z_{0}=ti$, where $t$ is a non-zero real number. Show that $r=pq$ and that $q>0$.

[4]

(c)

Hence determine the value of $k$ for which $z^{3}-3z^{2}+kz-12$ has a root of the form $ti$ with $t\neq0$, and find all three roots in that case.

[4]

(d)

Determine all real values of $m$ for which $z^{3}+mz^{2}+mz+1$ has a non-real purely imaginary root, and find all the roots of the cubic in each such case.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Since $p$, $q$ and $r$ are real, conjugating the equation $P(z_{0})=0$ gives $\overline{P(z_{0})}=0$. Conjugation respects sums and products with real coefficients, so $\overline{P(z_{0})}=P(\bar z_{0})$. (M1) Hence $P(\bar z_{0})=0$, so $\bar z_{0}$ is also a root. (A1)

If $z_{0}$ is non-real then $z_{0}\neq\bar z_{0}$, so $P$ has at least the two distinct non-real roots $z_{0}$ and $\bar z_{0}$. A cubic has exactly three roots counted with multiplicity; if the third root were also non-real, its conjugate would be a fourth root. Hence the third root is real, so $P$ has exactly one real root. (R1)(A1)

(b) Let $z_{0}=ti$ with $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $t\neq0$. Substituting,

$$P(ti)=(ti)^{3}+p(ti)^{2}+q(ti)+r=-t^{3}i-pt^{2}+qti+r.$$ (M1)

So $P(ti)=\left(r-pt^{2}\right)+\left(qt-t^{3}\right)i=0$, and both the real and imaginary parts must vanish. (A1)

The imaginary part gives $t(q-t^{2})=0$; since $t\neq0$ this forces $t^{2}=q$, and therefore $q=t^{2}>0$. (A1) The real part gives $r-pt^{2}=0$, so $r=pt^{2}=pq$. (A1) *(AG)*

(c) Here $p=-3$, $q=k$ and $r=-12$. The condition $r=pq$ becomes $-12=-3k$, so $k=4$, and $q=k=4>0$ is satisfied. (M1)(A1) Then $t^{2}=q=4$, so the purely imaginary roots are $\pm2i$. The third root is real and equals $-p=3$, since the sum of the roots of $z^{3}+pz^{2}+qz+r$ is $-p$. (M1) Indeed $(z-3)(z^{2}+4)=z^{3}-3z^{2}+4z-12$, so the roots are $3$, $2i$ and $-2i$. (A1)

(d) For $z^{3}+mz^{2}+mz+1$ we have $p=m$, $q=m$ and $r=1$. The necessary condition $r=pq$ gives $1=m^{2}$, so $m=\pm1$. (M1)(A1) But the condition from (b) also requires $q>0$, that is $m>0$, so $m=-1$ must be rejected. (M1)

Indeed for $m=-1$ the cubic is $z^{3}-z^{2}-z+1=(z-1)^{2}(z+1)$, whose roots $1$, $1$ and $-1$ are all real, so it has no purely imaginary root. (A1) Hence the only admissible value is $m=1$, and then $z^{3}+z^{2}+z+1=(z+1)(z^{2}+1)$, with roots $-1$, $i$ and $-i$. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The conjugate-root theorem is usually met as a fact to quote. Here it is used three times in different ways, and the last use separates candidates who understand it from those who have memorised it.

Part (a) is the theorem itself, with a small but real subtlety: the deduction that there is exactly one real root uses the fact that a cubic has three roots counted with multiplicity, so a non-real root consumes its conjugate as a second root and leaves precisely one. Students who argue from the graph, or who say 'the other roots are complex' without counting, miss the point.

Part (b) is the technical heart. Substituting $z=ti$ splits the cubic into a real part and an imaginary part, and the imaginary part factors as $t(q-t^{2})$. Because the root is assumed non-zero, $t\neq0$, and this forces $q=t^{2}>0$. The real part then forces $r=pt^{2}=pq$. So the single algebraic condition $r=pq$, together with the inequality $q>0$, is necessary for a purely imaginary root.

Part (c) applies the condition to a concrete cubic and produces the clean factorisation $(z-3)(z^{2}+4)$.

Part (d) is the lever. The condition $r=pq$ alone admits two values, $m=\pm1$, because $r=pq$ becomes $1=m^{2}$. The inequality $q>0$ is not decoration: it is what removes $m=-1$. And the reason is visible when the rejected case is factored, since $z^{3}-z^{2}-z+1$ has roots $1,1,-1$, all real, so it has no purely imaginary root at all. A candidate who treats $r=pq$ as sufficient will confidently answer $m=\pm1$ and be wrong.

The classic wrong turns are: forgetting that a non-real root is a pair; dividing by $t$ without recording that $t\neq0$; using only $r=pq$ and ignoring $q>0$ in (d); and mis-signing Vieta, since the sum of the roots of $z^{3}+pz^{2}+qz+r$ is $-p$, not $p$. A useful check is that $(z+p)(z^{2}+q)=z^{3}+pz^{2}+qz+pq$ reproduces the cubic exactly, which is why the condition is both necessary and sufficient.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.6 The quadratic function
questions.question:
For each real number $m$, define $f(x)=(m-1)x^{2}+2(m+1)x+(m+2)$. The family of curves $y=f(x)$ changes character as $m$ varies, and several parts of this question ask you to describe that change.

(a)

Show that when $m=1$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is a straight line, and state its equation.

[3]

(b)

For $m\neq1$, find the coordinates of the vertex of $y=f(x)$, giving your answer in terms of $m$.

[5]

(c)

Determine the set of values of $m$ for which the graph of $y=f(x)$ does not meet the $x$-axis.

[5]

(d)

Explain why, for every $m>1$, the vertex lies below the $x$-axis, and deduce the number of real roots of $f(x)=0$.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Setting $m=1$ makes the coefficient of $x^{2}$ equal to zero, so the quadratic degenerates to a linear expression (M1). Substituting gives $f(x)=2(1+1)x+(1+2)=4x+3$ (A1). Hence the graph is the straight line $y=4x+3$ (A1) *(AG)*. The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is the only term that can vanish, so this is the single value at which the family changes type.

(b) Completing the square for $m\neq1$, write $f(x)=(m-1)\left[x^{2}+\frac{2(m+1)}{m-1}x\right]+(m+2)$ (M1). The bracket becomes $\left(x+\frac{m+1}{m-1}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{m+1}{m-1}\right)^{2}$ (A1), so the axis of symmetry is $x=-\frac{m+1}{m-1}$ (A1). Substituting this value and simplifying gives $-\frac{m+3}{m-1}$ (M1)(A1). The vertex is therefore $\left(-\frac{m+1}{m-1},-\frac{m+3}{m-1}\right)$. This is the standard vertex formula for a parabola, and it is valid for every value of $m$ except the one excluded by the question.

(c) The discriminant is $[2(m+1)]^{2}-4(m-1)(m+2)$ (M1) $=4(m+1)^{2}-4(m-1)(m+2)$ (A1) $=4(m+3)$ (A1). The graph misses the $x$-axis exactly when the discriminant is negative, so $4(m+3)<0$ (M1), giving $m<-3$ (A1). Because the discriminant is linear in $m$, its sign changes at exactly one value, so the set of such $m$ is a single ray rather than a bounded interval.

(d) For $m>1$ the leading coefficient $m-1$ is positive, so the parabola opens upwards (A1). The $y$-coordinate of the vertex is $-\frac{m+3}{m-1}$, and both $m+3$ and $m-1$ are positive, so this value is negative (R1). An upward parabola whose vertex lies below the $x$-axis must cross the axis twice (M1), so $f(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots (A1), consistent with $4(m+3)>0$. The sign of the discriminant gives independent confirmation of this count, so the number of real roots is exactly two.
questions.explanation:
The trap is that the leading coefficient depends on the parameter. Most candidates treat $f$ as a quadratic throughout, and part (a) is designed to catch exactly that: when $m=1$ there is no $x^{2}$ term at all, and the curve is a line. A candidate who divides by $m-1$ without first checking that $m\neq1$ will produce an undefined vertex.

The second trap is the discriminant. Expanding $[2(m+1)]^{2}-4(m-1)(m+2)$ is routine, but the cancellation is delicate: the $m^{2}$ terms disappear and leave the linear expression $4(m+3)$. Candidates who lose a factor of four, or who expand $(m-1)(m+2)$ carelessly, will get the wrong threshold. The correct reading is that the sign of the discriminant is controlled entirely by $m+3$, so the boundary is at $m=-3$, not at $m=1$ or $m=0$.

Part (d) is a reasoning question that rewards understanding the shape of a parabola. The vertex formula from part (b) is reused, but the point is not to compute anything new: it is to notice that an upward-opening parabola whose lowest point is below the axis has to cross the axis on both sides. The discriminant from part (c) confirms this, since $m>1$ makes $4(m+3)$ positive.

Classic wrong turns include assuming the family is always a parabola; writing the vertex with the wrong signs; treating 'does not meet the $x$-axis' as 'discriminant less than or equal to zero'; and in part (d) concluding that there are no real roots because the vertex is negative. A candidate who sketches the family for two or three values of $m$ will see the transition from a line at $m=1$ to very narrow parabolas for values of $m$ close to one. The family is a useful illustration of how a single parameter can change the nature of a curve.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.9 Exponential functions and their graphs and 2.10 Solving equations analytically
questions.question:
Let $f(x)=3^{x}$ and $g(x)=3^{-x}$.

(a)

Sketch the graphs of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ on the same axes, stating the equation of the asymptote and the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of each.

[4]

(b)

Show that the graph of $y=g(x)$ is the reflection of the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the $y$-axis, and find the coordinates of their point of intersection.

[4]

(c)

Find the two transformations that map the graph of $y=f(x)$ onto the graph of $y=3^{x-2}+1$, and state the equation of the asymptote and the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of the image.

[4]

(d)

Determine the set of values of $k$ for which $3^{2x}-4\cdot3^{x}+k=0$ has two distinct real solutions.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Both curves have the negative $x$-axis as a horizontal asymptote, that is $y=0$ (A1). Since $3^{0}=1$, both pass through $(0,1)$ (A1). The graph of $f$ rises from left to right without bound, while the graph of $g$ falls from left to right, tending to zero (A1)(A1). Both curves lie entirely above the $x$-axis, so neither ever meets it, and the only point they share is the intercept.

(b) Replacing $x$ by $-x$ in $f$ gives $f(-x)=3^{-x}=g(x)$ (M1)(A1), so $g$ is the reflection of $f$ in the $y$-axis. At an intersection $3^{x}=3^{-x}$ (M1), so $3^{2x}=1$ and hence $x=0$ (A1); the point is $(0,1)$. The reflection is a symmetry of this particular pair of curves, and it does not depend on the value of the base.

(c) We have $3^{x-2}+1=f(x-2)+1$. The graph of $f(x-2)$ is obtained by translating $y=f(x)$ by $2$ units in the positive $x$-direction (A1), and adding $1$ translates the result by $1$ unit in the positive $y$-direction (A1). The asymptote $y=0$ moves to $y=1$ (A1), and the $y$-intercept is $3^{0-2}+1=\frac{1}{9}+1=\frac{10}{9}$, that is $\left(0,\frac{10}{9}\right)$ (A1). Because both operations are translations, their order is immaterial, and the image is the same curve either way.

(d) Put $u=3^{x}$, so $u>0$ and the equation becomes $u^{2}-4u+k=0$ (M1). Two distinct real solutions in $x$ require two distinct positive roots $u$ (R1). The discriminant $16-4k$ must be positive, giving $k<4$ (M1)(A1), and the product of the roots, equal to $k$, must be positive, giving $k>0$ (A1). Hence $0<k<4$ (A1). The product condition is the one that is easily overlooked, and it is what removes the negative values of $k$ from the answer.
questions.explanation:
The question concerns two exponential curves that are mirror images of each other, but the difficulty is concentrated in the final part, where a hidden quadratic in $3^{x}$ appears. Parts (a) to (c) are standard graph work and are there to establish the vocabulary of asymptote, intercept and transformation before the algebraic twist.

The most common error is in part (d). Candidates set the discriminant of $u^{2}-4u+k=0$ to be positive, obtain $k<4$, and stop. That is necessary but not sufficient: the substitution $u=3^{x}$ restricts $u$ to positive values, so both roots of the quadratic must be positive. For a quadratic with leading coefficient one, the product of the roots equals $k$, so positivity of the product gives $k>0$. The sum of the roots is $4$, which is positive automatically, so no further condition is needed. The answer is therefore the open interval $0<k<4$.

A candidate who reasons only about the discriminant will include negative values of $k$ in the answer. At $k=-1$, for instance, the quadratic $u^{2}-4u-1=0$ has one positive and one negative root, and only the positive root corresponds to a real $x$, so there is exactly one solution rather than two. This is the fastest numerical check.

Other traps include treating the asymptote of $3^{x-2}+1$ as $y=0$; computing the $y$-intercept as $3^{-2}$ and forgetting the $+1$; and in part (b) assuming the curves meet where the graph crosses the axis. The base three is a red herring, since every positive base other than one behaves in the same way and the structure of the answer does not depend on it. The base is arbitrary, so the result is really a statement about all exponential functions whose base is greater than one.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 3.1 The distance between two points in three-dimensional space
questions.question:
The points $A(1,0,2)$, $B(3,4,0)$ and $C(5,8,-2)$ are given, and $O$ denotes the origin. Each part below refers to these three points and to the vectors that join them.

(a)

Show that the points $A(1,0,2)$, $B(3,4,0)$ and $C(5,8,-2)$ are collinear.

[4]

(b)

Find the distance $AC$, giving your answer in the form $k\sqrt{6}$ where $k$ is a positive integer.

[4]

(c)

Find the coordinates of the point $P$ on the segment $AC$ such that $AP:PC=1:3$.

[4]

(d)

Determine the coordinates of the two points on the line through $A$ and $C$ whose distance from the origin is exactly three units.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The vector $\overrightarrow{AB}=(3-1,4-0,0-2)=(2,4,-2)$ (M1) and $\overrightarrow{BC}=(5-3,8-4,-2-0)=(2,4,-2)$ (A1). The two vectors are equal, so the segments $AB$ and $BC$ are parallel (R1). Since they also share the point $B$, the three points must lie on one straight line (A1)(AG). Equal displacement vectors force $A$, $B$ and $C$ onto a single line, and no other arrangement of the points is consistent with the two vectors just found.

(b) The vector $\overrightarrow{AC}=(5-1,8-0,-2-2)=(4,8,-4)$ (M1). By the distance formula, $AC=\sqrt{4^{2}+8^{2}+(-4)^{2}}$ (M1) $=\sqrt{16+64+16}=\sqrt{96}$ (A1) $=4\sqrt{6}$ (A1), so $k=4$. The factor $16$ inside the root is what produces the exact surd form rather than a decimal. The distance formula used here is simply the three-dimensional form of Pythagoras applied to the three coordinate differences.

(c) Since $AP:PC=1:3$, the point $P$ divides $AC$ internally in that ratio, so $P=A+\frac{1}{4}(C-A)$ (M1). Now $\frac{1}{4}(C-A)=\frac{1}{4}(4,8,-4)=(1,2,-1)$ (A1), hence $P=(1,0,2)+(1,2,-1)$ (A1) $=(2,2,1)$ (A1). The ratio places $P$ one quarter of the way from $A$ towards $C$. The fraction multiplies the whole vector $C-A$, so reversing the ratio would place the point three quarters of the way along instead.

(d) A general point of the line is $(1+4t,8t,2-4t)$ (M1). Its squared distance from $O$ is $(1+4t)^{2}+(8t)^{2}+(2-4t)^{2}$ (M1) $=96t^{2}-8t+5$ (A1). Setting this equal to $9$ gives $96t^{2}-8t-4=0$, that is $24t^{2}-2t-1=0$ (M1), so $t=\frac{1}{4}$ or $t=-\frac{1}{6}$ (A1). The two points are therefore $(2,2,1)$ and $\left(\frac{1}{3},-\frac{4}{3},\frac{8}{3}\right)$ (A1); the first of these is exactly the point $P$ found in part (c) (R1). The negative root describes the point reached by travelling in the opposite direction from $A$, away from $C$, and it lies on the same infinite line.
questions.explanation:
The first three parts are deliberately gentle so that the final part can carry the difficulty. Parts (a) and (b) ask for collinearity and a distance, which most candidates can do, and part (c) introduces the point $P$ that will reappear at the end. The lever is the final part: the line is fixed by $A$ and $C$, and the question asks for the points on that line at a given distance from a point that does not lie on it. Candidates who try to solve this by inspection or by drawing will not find the second point.

The natural route is to parametrise the line as $A+t(C-A)=(1+4t,8t,2-4t)$ and then impose $|OP|^{2}=9$. Expanding gives the quadratic $96t^{2}-8t+5$, and setting it equal to $9$ gives $24t^{2}-2t-1=0$, whose roots are $t=\frac{1}{4}$ and $t=-\frac{1}{6}$. The two roots correspond to the two points, one lying between $A$ and $C$ and one beyond $A$ on the other side. A candidate who assumes the answer lies on the segment $AC$ will find only $(2,2,1)$ and lose the final marks.

The most common error is to set the distance rather than the squared distance equal to $9$, which introduces a square root and hides the quadratic. Another is to use a parameter measured from $O$ instead of along $AC$. The appearance of $P$ as one of the two solutions is the intended check: it confirms that the algebra is consistent with part (c) and rewards candidates who notice the connection rather than treating the parts as unrelated. A candidate who has met only two-dimensional coordinate geometry will find the arithmetic familiar, but the extra coordinate is what makes the parametrisation of the line the natural tool rather than a sketch.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 3.4 The circle: radian measure of angles, length of an arc and area of a sector
questions.question:
A sector of a circle has radius $r$ cm and angle $\theta$ radians, and its perimeter is $20$ cm. All angles in this question are to be given in radians.

(a)

Show that the area $A$ cm$^{2}$ of the sector is given by $A=10r-r^{2}$.

[4]

(b)

Determine the value of $r$ for which $A$ is greatest, and state the greatest value of $A$.

[4]

(c)

Find, for $r=5$, the value of $\theta$ in radians and the length of the arc.

[4]

(d)

Determine the two values of $r$ for which $A=16$, and explain why only one of them is possible.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The perimeter of the sector is $2r+r\theta=20$ (M1), so $r\theta=20-2r$ (A1). The area is $A=\frac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{2}r(r\theta)$ (M1) $=\frac{1}{2}r(20-2r)=10r-r^{2}$ (A1)(AG). Writing the area this way removes $\theta$ entirely and leaves a single-variable expression. The substitution is the whole idea of the first part: once the angle has been eliminated, the problem becomes a question about a single variable, and the fixed perimeter is the constraint that makes the elimination possible.

(b) Completing the square, $A=10r-r^{2}=25-(r-5)^{2}$ (M1)(A1). Since $(r-5)^{2}\ge 0$, the area is greatest when $r=5$ (A1), and the greatest value is $A=25$ cm$^{2}$ (A1). The value $r=5$ gives a genuine maximum rather than a minimum because the coefficient of $r^{2}$ is negative, so the parabola opens downwards. Completing the square is preferred to differentiation here because it displays the maximum and the value at which it occurs at the same time.

(c) Substituting $r=5$ into $r\theta=20-2r$ gives $5\theta=10$ (M1), so $\theta=2$ radians (A1). The arc length is $r\theta=5\cdot 2=10$ cm (M1)(A1). The angle of two radians is slightly less than a third of a full turn, and the arc length of ten centimetres is exactly half the fixed perimeter.

(d) Setting $10r-r^{2}=16$ gives $r^{2}-10r+16=0$ (M1), so $(r-2)(r-8)=0$ and $r=2$ or $r=8$ (A1). For $r=2$ the angle would be $\theta=\frac{20-4}{2}=8$ radians (A1), which exceeds $2\pi\approx 6.28$, so no such sector exists. For $r=8$ the angle is $\theta=\frac{20-16}{8}=0.5$ radians, which is admissible (R1), so only $r=8$ survives. The two roots are found by factorising, which is straightforward because their sum is ten and their product is sixteen. Only the geometric constraint removes the smaller one.
questions.explanation:
The sector is a standard optimisation, but the final part turns it into a question about which of two algebraic solutions is geometrically real. The perimeter is fixed at $20$ cm, so the radius and the angle are linked by $r\theta=20-2r$; the area then becomes the one-variable quadratic $10r-r^{2}$, whose maximum is $25$ cm$^{2}$ at $r=5$. Parts (a) to (c) are there to make that reduction explicit and to give the reader the tools needed for the last part.

The twist is that $A=16$ has two algebraic solutions, $r=2$ and $r=8$, but only one of them corresponds to a sector. The angle for $r=2$ is $\theta=8$ radians, which is larger than $2\pi$, and an angle greater than a full turn does not describe a simple sector. The angle for $r=8$ is $0.5$ radians, which is perfectly possible. The condition that must be checked is therefore $\theta\le 2\pi$, or equivalently $r\ge\frac{20}{2+2\pi}$, and it is not visible in the quadratic itself.

Candidates who stop at the two roots will report both and lose the reasoning mark. The same check explains why the maximum at $r=5$ gives $\theta=2$ radians, comfortably within range. A useful sanity check is to substitute each radius back into the perimeter: $2(2)+2(8)=20$ and $2(8)+8(0.5)=20$ both hold, so the perimeter alone cannot distinguish the two cases; only the constraint on the angle can. The numbers $20$, $16$ and the radius $5$ were chosen so that the quadratic factors over the integers and the maximum is exact. The maximum area of twenty-five square centimetres occurs at a radius of five centimetres, which is exactly a quarter of the fixed perimeter. The angle constraint is easy to forget in a purely algebraic treatment.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.1 Concepts of population, sample, random sample
questions.question:
Nine masses, in grams, are recorded as $5$, $6$, $7$, $8$, $9$, $10$, $11$, $12$ and $40$. The values are treated as a sample from a larger population of recorded masses.

(a)

Explain what is meant by a random sample in this context, and give one reason why a random sample is preferred to a convenience sample.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the mean and the median of the nine recorded masses, and comment on what the comparison between them suggests about the shape of the distribution.

[4]

(c)

Show, using the interquartile range, that the value $40$ is an outlier; you should state both quartiles and the boundary you use.

[4]

(d)

The value $40$ is found to be a recording error and is removed; determine the new mean and the new median, and explain why the median moves less than the mean.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection, independently of the others (M1). The population here is every mass that could have been recorded, and a random sample would select nine items using a random generator (A1). A convenience sample takes the items easiest to reach, so awkward items are excluded and the sample is not representative (R1). That exclusion biases any estimate from the data, whereas random selection keeps the sample representative (A1). Random selection makes the summary trustworthy.

(b) Adding the nine values gives $5+6+7+8+9+10+11+12+40=108$ (M1), so the mean is $\frac{108}{9}=12$ (A1). In order, the fifth value is $9$, so the median is $9$ (A1). The mean lies above the median, suggesting a tail towards the larger values, because one large value lifts the mean without moving the middle (R1). The comparison indicates skew.

(c) With nine ordered values the lower quartile is the mean of the second and third, $\frac{6+7}{2}=6.5$ (M1), and the upper quartile is the mean of the seventh and eighth, $\frac{11+12}{2}=11.5$ (A1). The interquartile range is $11.5-6.5=5$ (A1). The upper boundary is $Q_3+1.5\times IQR=11.5+7.5=19$, and since $40>19$ the value $40$ is an outlier (A1)(AG). The standard $1.5$ IQR rule places $40$ far outside this boundary.

(d) Removing $40$ leaves $n=8$ and a total of $108-40=68$ (M1), so the new mean is $\frac{68}{8}=8.5$ (A1). The new median is the mean of the fourth and fifth values, $\frac{8+9}{2}=8.5$ (A1). The mean falls by $3.5$ while the median falls by only $0.5$, because the mean uses the size of every value and reacts to the outlier, while the median depends only on position (R1). This difference separates the two averages.
questions.explanation:
This item turns on the difference between two measures of centre when one value is wrong. The nine masses are deliberately almost symmetric, running from $5$ to $12$, so that the mean and median would agree at $8.5$ were it not for the final entry. That entry, $40$, is far larger than the rest and lifts the mean to $12$ while leaving the median at $9$. The gap of three grams is produced by one recording.

The intended route is to sum the values, divide by nine, order them and read off the fifth. Part (c) then applies the $1.5$ IQR rule, which is the only reason the value $40$ can be labelled an outlier rather than merely large. Candidates who compute the quartiles by splitting the ordered list into four equal groups often mishandle nine values, since the groups cannot be equal; the convention used here takes the median of each half, giving $6.5$ and $11.5$.

Part (d) turns the comparison into an argument. Removing $40$ gives a mean of $8.5$ and a median of $8.5$, so the two measures now coincide exactly. The reason the mean moved further is that it is computed from every value, so a single extreme observation carries weight, whereas the median is fixed by the position of the middle and only shifts when the count changes. The classic error is to remove the outlier and then recompute the median from the remaining eight values by taking the fourth alone; with an even count the median is the mean of the two central values, here $\frac{8+9}{2}=8.5$. A candidate who treats the outlier as genuine keeps the inflated mean and reaches the opposite conclusion about the shape.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.2 Presentation of data (discrete and continuous)
questions.question:
One hundred observations are grouped into five classes of unequal width. The classes and their frequencies are $0\le x<2$ with frequency $12$, $2\le x<4$ with frequency $8$, $4\le x<8$ with frequency $40$, $8\le x<12$ with frequency $24$, and $12\le x<20$ with frequency $16$.

(a)

Explain why frequency alone cannot be plotted on the vertical axis when the class widths differ, and calculate the frequency density of each of the five classes.

[4]

(b)

Show that the median lies in the class $4\le x<8$, and estimate its value.

[4]

(c)

Estimate the interquartile range, showing clearly the positions you use.

[4]

(d)

Estimate the 90th percentile and interpret it in the context of the observations.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) With unequal widths a tall bar shows a wide class, not a crowded one, so the axis must show frequency per unit of width (M1). Frequency density is frequency divided by class width, so the five densities are $\frac{12}{2}=6$ (A1), $\frac{8}{2}=4$ and $\frac{40}{4}=10$ (A1), then $\frac{24}{4}=6$ and $\frac{16}{8}=2$ (A1). The tallest bar is the class $4\le x<8$, with density $10$, although its width is only four. Density, not frequency, is comparable across unequal widths.

(b) The total frequency is $100$, so the median is at position $50$ (M1). The cumulative frequencies are $12$, $20$, $60$, $84$ and $100$, so the fiftieth value falls in the class $4\le x<8$ (A1). Within that class, $30$ of the $40$ observations are needed (M1), so the median is $4+\frac{30}{40}\times 4=7$ (A1). This assumes an even spread in the class.

(c) The lower quartile lies at position $25$ (M1). The cumulative frequency reaches $20$ at $x=4$, so $5$ more come from the class of width $4$, giving $Q_1=4+\frac{5}{40}\times 4=4.5$ (A1). The upper quartile lies at position $75$, and the cumulative frequency reaches $60$ at $x=8$, so $Q_3=8+\frac{15}{24}\times 4=10.5$ (A1). The interquartile range is $10.5-4.5=6$ (A1). Each quartile uses the same interpolation as the median.

(d) The ninetieth percentile lies at position $90$ (M1). The cumulative frequency reaches $84$ at $x=12$, so $6$ observations come from the class $12\le x<20$ of width $8$ and frequency $16$, giving $P_{90}=12+\frac{6}{16}\times 8=15$ (A1)(A1). In context, about ninety per cent lie below $15$, so ten per cent exceed it (A1). The value is an estimate, again assuming an even spread in the top class.
questions.explanation:
The item turns on frequency and frequency density answering different questions. The class $4\le x<8$ contains the largest frequency, $40$, but a narrower class can be equally crowded per unit of width: the class $0\le x<2$ has density $6$, against $10$ for the wide class. A candidate who simply plots the frequencies produces a histogram whose areas no longer represent the data, because a bar of height $40$ over a width of four claims an area of $160$ observations. The densities $6$, $4$, $10$, $6$ and $2$ restore the property that each area equals the frequency it represents.

The cumulative frequencies are needed for the median and the quartiles, and the key step is to convert a position into an interpolation within a class. For the median the position is $50$, which lies in the third class; the fraction is $\frac{50-20}{40}$, and multiplying by the class width of four gives an addition of three, so the median is $7$. The quartiles use positions $25$ and $75$ in the same way, and the percentile uses position $90$.

The common error is to assume that the median is the midpoint of the class containing it, which would give $6$ and is wrong because the observations are not evenly distributed within the class boundary. Another error is to use cumulative frequencies rather than positions, or to take $Q_3$ from the fourth class when the cumulative frequency of $75$ still lies in the third. The class limits were chosen so that each interpolation fraction is simple: $\frac{30}{40}$, $\frac{5}{40}$, $\frac{15}{24}$ and $\frac{6}{16}$ all reduce to tidy quarters or eighths, so a correct method produces exact values while a mistaken one usually does not.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.3 Measures of central tendency and dispersion
questions.question:
The data set $A$ is $\{4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$, and the set $B$ is obtained from $A$ by the coding $b=2a-6$. In the final parts a different set $x$ is coded as $w=1.5x-4$.

(a)

Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the set $A$.

[4]

(b)

Determine the mean and the standard deviation of the coded values $2a-6$, and explain why the mean changes by the whole transformation while the standard deviation is affected only by the multiplicative part.

[4]

(c)

A different set $x$ is coded as $w=1.5x-4$, and the coded values have mean $14$ and standard deviation $4.5$. Find the mean and the standard deviation of $x$.

[4]

(d)

Explain why subtracting $4$ leaves the standard deviation unchanged while multiplying by $1.5$ multiplies it, and give one reason a researcher might code data.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The mean of $A$ is $\frac{4+5+6+7+8}{5}=6$ (M1)(A1). The deviations from the mean are $-2$, $-1$, $0$, $1$ and $2$, whose squares are $4$, $1$, $0$, $1$ and $4$ (M1). The variance is $\frac{10}{5}=2$, so the standard deviation is $\sqrt{2}=1.41$ to three significant figures (A1). The divisor is $5$ because these values are treated as the whole population.

(b) Coding with $b=2a-6$ gives $2$, $4$, $6$, $8$ and $10$, whose mean is $\frac{30}{5}=6$ (M1)(A1). The deviations are doubled, so each squared deviation is multiplied by $4$ and the variance becomes $4\times 2=8$ (M1), giving a standard deviation of $\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}=2.83$ (A1). The mean changes by the whole transformation because every value is shifted and scaled, while the standard deviation ignores the shift of $-6$ and is scaled only by the factor $2$.

(c) Since the coding is $w=1.5x-4$, the mean satisfies $14=1.5\bar{x}-4$ (M1), so $1.5\bar{x}=18$ and $\bar{x}=12$ (A1). The standard deviation is unaffected by the subtraction of $4$, so $4.5=1.5\sigma_x$ (M1), giving $\sigma_x=\frac{4.5}{1.5}=3$ (A1). The inverse transformation is obtained by solving the coding rule rather than applying it again.

(d) Subtracting $4$ translates every value by the same amount, so all deviations from the mean are unchanged and the standard deviation is unchanged (M1)(A1). Multiplying by $1.5$ scales every deviation by $1.5$, so the variance is multiplied by $1.5^2$ and the standard deviation by $1.5$ (A1). A researcher might code data to remove an awkward constant, such as a large offset, so that the numbers are easier to handle later (R1). Only the multiplicative part of the coding changes the spread.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the algebra of constant changes to a data set. For set $A$ the mean is $6$ and the variance is $2$. Coding by $b=2a-6$ produces the set $2$, $4$, $6$, $8$, $10$, which has the same mean of $6$ but a variance of $8$. The two sets therefore sit at exactly the same place on the number line while the second is visibly more spread out, which is the contrast the title names.

The intended route separates the two parts of a linear coding. A shift of $-6$ moves every value by the same amount, so every deviation from the mean is unchanged and the standard deviation is untouched. A multiplier of $2$ scales every deviation by $2$, so each squared deviation is scaled by $4$ and the variance by $4$; the standard deviation, being a square root, is scaled by $2$ alone. This is why $\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}$.

Part (c) reverses the direction. Given the coded mean $14$ and the coded standard deviation $4.5$, the candidate must solve $14=1.5\bar{x}-4$ and $4.5=1.5\sigma_x$, obtaining $12$ and $3$. The common error is to apply the coding rule again rather than invert it, which produces a mean of $17$ instead of $12$. A second error is to divide by $1.5^2$ rather than $1.5$ when recovering the standard deviation, confusing variance with standard deviation. The numbers were chosen so that the coded mean equals the original mean, which disguises the shift, and so that the inverse values are whole numbers.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.5 Concepts of trial, outcome, equally likely outcomes, sample space
questions.question:
Two different numbers are chosen at random from the set $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$. In the final part the two numbers are chosen with replacement.

(a)

Determine the sample space of all pairs of different numbers, and state the number of equally likely outcomes.

[4]

(b)

Find the probability that the larger of the two numbers is exactly $3$.

[4]

(c)

Find the probability that the larger number is at least $3$ and the smaller number is odd.

[4]

(d)

The two numbers are now chosen with replacement; determine the probability that the two numbers are equal, and explain how the sample space changes.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Choosing two different numbers from four gives $\binom{4}{2}=6$ pairs, namely $\{1,2\}$, $\{1,3\}$, $\{1,4\}$, $\{2,3\}$, $\{2,4\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ (M1)(A1). Because each pair is equally likely and order does not matter, each outcome has probability $\frac{1}{6}$ (A1). The sample space therefore contains six equally likely outcomes, and every event can be counted directly from this list (A1). The unordered convention avoids counting each pair twice.

(b) The larger number is exactly $3$ in the pairs $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ (M1)(A1). There are two such outcomes out of six, so the probability is $\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}$ (A1). The outcome $\{3,4\}$ is excluded because its larger number is $4$, not $3$ (R1). The count is a direct enumeration, so no multiplication rule is needed.

(c) The condition requires the larger number to be at least $3$ and the smaller number to be odd. The qualifying pairs are $\{1,3\}$, $\{1,4\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ (M1)(A1), giving three outcomes out of six, so the probability is $\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$ (A1). The pair $\{2,3\}$ fails because its smaller number, $2$, is even (R1). Checking each pair against both conditions is the only reliable way to count this event.

(d) With replacement each of the two choices is made from four numbers, giving $4\times 4=16$ equally likely ordered outcomes (M1)(A1). The two numbers are equal in the four outcomes $(1,1)$, $(2,2)$, $(3,3)$ and $(4,4)$, so the probability is $\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}$ (A1). The space now contains ordered pairs and repeated values, so it is larger and its outcomes are different from before (R1). Replacement is what makes the two choices independent.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the concepts of trial, outcome, sample space and event, and it uses a space small enough to enumerate but phrased so that careless counting fails. Two different numbers are chosen from four, giving six unordered pairs. The sample space is fixed and finite, and each outcome is equally likely, so every probability in the first three parts is a simple ratio of counts.

The first subtlety is that the pairs are unordered. If a candidate lists ordered pairs there are twelve, and each has probability $\frac{1}{12}$; the probabilities are unchanged, but the counts double and the arithmetic must be adjusted. The convention should be stated before counting begins, because mixing the two conventions is the most common source of error.

Part (b) asks for the larger number to be exactly three, which is true of $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ only. Part (c) adds a second condition, that the smaller number is odd, and the qualifying pairs are $\{1,3\}$, $\{1,4\}$ and $\{3,4\}$. The pair $\{2,3\}$ looks promising because its larger number is three, but its smaller number is even, so it is excluded. This is the conditional phrasing that hides the answer: a candidate who counts only on the larger number obtains the wrong event.

Part (d) changes the trial by allowing replacement. The sample space becomes the sixteen ordered pairs, repeated values are now possible, and the event that the two numbers are equal has probability $\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}$. The numbers were chosen so that the probabilities are the simple fractions $\frac{1}{6}$, $\frac{1}{3}$, $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$, and so that the excluded pair in part (c) is genuinely tempting. Replacement is the lever that rebuilds the space.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.6 Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, sample space diagrams and tables of outcomes
questions.question:
Two events $H$ and $G$ in the same sample space satisfy $P(H)=0.6$, $P(G)=0.45$ and $P(H\cap G)=0.25$. Each part below refers to these two events.

(a)

Find $P(H\cup G)$, the probability that at least one of the two events occurs.

[4]

(b)

Find $P(H\mid G)$ and $P(G\mid H)$, giving each answer as an exact fraction in its lowest terms.

[4]

(c)

Determine, showing your reasoning, whether the events $H$ and $G$ are independent.

[4]

(d)

Given that at least one of $H$ and $G$ occurs, find the probability that both occur.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The addition rule for two events gives $P(H\cup G)=P(H)+P(G)-P(H\cap G)$ (M1) $=0.6+0.45-0.25$ (A1) $=0.8$ (A1), so the probability that at least one of the two events occurs is $0.8$ (A1). The subtraction is needed because the outcomes lying in both events would otherwise be counted twice, so the rule is valid for any two events in the same sample space, whether or not those events are independent.

(b) The conditional probability formula gives $P(H\mid G)=\frac{P(H\cap G)}{P(G)}=\frac{0.25}{0.45}$ (M1) $=\frac{25}{45}=\frac{5}{9}$ (A1). Applying the same formula the other way round, $P(G\mid H)=\frac{P(H\cap G)}{P(H)}=\frac{0.25}{0.6}$ (M1) $=\frac{25}{60}=\frac{5}{12}$ (A1). Each conditional probability restricts attention to the conditioning event, so its denominator is the probability of that event alone, which is why the two fractions differ even though both use the same joint probability.

(c) Two events are independent precisely when $P(H\cap G)=P(H)P(G)$ (M1). Here $P(H)P(G)=0.6\times 0.45=0.27$ (A1), and this is not equal to the given value $0.25$ (R1). Hence $H$ and $G$ are not independent (A1), because the product of the separate probabilities fails to reproduce the joint probability.

(d) Conditioning on the union restricts the sample space to $H\cup G$ (M1), so the required probability is $\frac{P(H\cap G)}{P(H\cup G)}$ (A1) $=\frac{0.25}{0.8}$ (A1) $=\frac{25}{80}=\frac{5}{16}=0.3125$ (A1). This conditioning event is the union rather than a single event, so the quantity is different from either answer in part (b), and the calculation is correct because the definition of conditional probability applies to any event of positive probability.
questions.explanation:
The item turns on the difference between conditioning on one event and conditioning on the union of two events. Parts (a) to (c) establish the familiar facts: the union has probability $0.8$, the two conditional probabilities are $\frac{5}{9}$ and $\frac{5}{12}$, and the events are dependent because $0.6$ times $0.45$ is $0.27$ rather than $0.25$. A candidate who has done the standard independence test will feel that part (c) has settled the matter.

Part (d) then asks for the probability of both events given that at least one occurs, which is $\frac{0.25}{0.8}=\frac{5}{16}=0.3125$. The lever is that the conditioning event is now the union, not a single event, so the earlier independence verdict gives no shortcut: a candidate who reasons that dependent events must reduce the conditional probability, or who tries to reuse $\frac{5}{9}$ or $\frac{5}{12}$, will not obtain the answer. The correct route is to apply the definition of conditional probability to the event $H\cup G$.

The common error is to treat at least one as though it were a single named event and to condition on $H$ or on $G$ instead, which produces $\frac{5}{9}$ or $\frac{5}{12}$ and answers a different question. A second error is to assume that dependence forces the conditional probability of both to be smaller than $0.25$, whereas it is in fact larger. The numbers $0.6$, $0.45$ and $0.25$ were chosen so that the union is exactly $0.8$ and the required fraction reduces to $\frac{5}{16}$, a value distinct from both conditional probabilities computed earlier.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.10 Equation of the regression line of x on y
questions.question:
Twelve pairs of data $(x,y)$ satisfy $\sum x=84$, $\sum y=60$, $\sum x^{2}=638$, $\sum y^{2}=380$ and $\sum xy=460$. A calculator is required throughout.

(a)

Show that $S_{xx}=50$ and $S_{xy}=40$.

[4]

(b)

Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$, giving it in the form $y=a+bx$.

[4]

(c)

Find the equation of the regression line of $x$ on $y$, giving it in the form $x=c+dy$.

[4]

(d)

A student rearranges the line from part (b) to make $x$ the subject and claims that this is the regression line of $x$ on $y$. Explain why the student is wrong.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The mean of $x$ is $\bar{x}=\frac{84}{12}=7$ (M1) and the mean of $y$ is $\bar{y}=\frac{60}{12}=5$ (A1). Then $S_{xx}=638-\frac{84^{2}}{12}=638-588=50$ (M1)(A1) and $S_{xy}=460-\frac{84\times 60}{12}=460-420=40$ (A1)(AG). These centred sums subtract the variation already accounted for by the means, so they measure spread about the mean rather than about the origin, which is why the printed values are correct.

(b) The gradient of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $b=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac{40}{50}=0.8$ (M1)(A1), and the intercept is $a=\bar{y}-b\bar{x}=5-0.8\times 7=-0.6$ (M1)(A1). Hence $y=-0.6+0.8x$ (A1). The line passes through the point of means $(7,5)$, which is what determines the intercept once the gradient is known.

(c) The gradient of the regression line of $x$ on $y$ uses $S_{yy}$, and $S_{yy}=380-\frac{60^{2}}{12}=80$ (M1)(A1). Therefore the gradient is $d=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}}=\frac{40}{80}=0.5$ (A1), and the intercept is $c=\bar{x}-d\bar{y}=7-0.5\times 5=4.5$ (M1), so $x=4.5+0.5y$ (A1). Exchanging the roles of the two variables replaces $S_{xx}$ by $S_{yy}$ in the denominator, which is why this gradient differs from the one in part (b).

(d) Rearranging the line from part (b) gives $x=\frac{y+0.6}{0.8}=1.25y+0.75$ (M1)(A1). This is not the regression line of $x$ on $y$, because that line minimises the squared deviations in $x$ and has gradient $\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}}=0.5$ (M1). The two lines coincide only when the correlation is exactly $\pm 1$, whereas here $r=\frac{40}{\sqrt{50\times 80}}=0.632$ (A1)(R1). Rearranging changes the subject of the formula but not which variable is treated as the response, so the student has reversed the equation without reversing the regression.
questions.explanation:
